speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REVISION OF SALARIES OF TEMPORARY EMPLOYEES
speechtext: I wish to inform the house that the commissioners of internal economy have reviewed the salaries of temporary employees of the House of Commons. It is my pleasure to report that they have authorized a revision of salaries in line with the increases being granted to civil servants. This decision conforms with our practice to the effect that in the past when general salary revisions have been granted to public service employees the salaries of our temporary employees have been adjusted, effective from the same date as that which has been announced for the coming into effect of the increased salaries of the civil servants.

maintopic: THE LATE J. W. NOSEWORTHY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE LATE J. W. NOSEWORTHY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of the house were saddened at the news we received during the Easter recess of the death of one of our colleagues, Mr. Joseph Noseworthy. The news came to us as a particularly startling shock, for only a few weeks before we had been happy to witness what seemed to be his successful and rapid recovery from an ailment which had kept him away from his desk for a few days earlier this session.
Mr. Noseworthy's career was one of many victories against heavy odds. He was in the true sense a self-made man who quietly and persistently overcame the obstacles that lay before him. The son of a Newfoundland fisherman, it was not until after he migrated to Canada in 1910 that he was able to work his way through college and university and complete the higher education which had always been his aim. Thereafter his rise in his profession as a teacher was rapid.
Within a few years he became the head of a department of a large collegiate in north Toronto. It was while serving in that post that his fellow teachers showed their appreciation of his professional and personal qualities by electing him president of the Ontario secondary school teachers federation, a position he held for nine years.
His very election to this house in a famous by-election in 1942 gave striking evidence of the way in which Mr. Noseworthy met and overcame difficulties. Since coming to this house he applied the full force of his talents in the promotion of the political and social principles in which he believed and he made many able contributions to a wide variety of debates in this chamber. Those of us who did not always agree with him in what he said nevertheless respected him for the sincerity with which he spoke and for the kindliness and courtesy of his relations with his fellow members.
To Mrs. Noseworthy and the members of the family who have lost a beloved husband and father and to the leader and members of his party who have lost a valued colleague, Mr. Speaker, we all extend, I am sure, our deepest sympathy.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: THE LATE J. W. NOSEWORTHY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in joining with the Prime Minister in the expression of regret and sympathy in the loss of a friend who was known to everyone here as a kind, gentle and very devoted member of this house, I feel that I should also repeat what the Prime Minister has said with regard to Mr. Noseworthy's return to this house earlier. The very fact that he did come back to the House of Commons after an earlier illness suggested the certainty that the damage of the attack he had suffered had not been too severe. I think every one of us looked with confidence to his continued good health.
Mr. Noseworthy brought to this house the warm, personal interest in the affairs of his own community that grew out of his service as a teacher in that community. On educational matters he spoke with authority; on other matters he spoke with the interests of those he served at heart.
I think it can be said that there was not a single member of this house who did not hold him in high, personal regard. I know that all of us are going to miss his contributions very greatly and will miss from

The late J. W. Noseworthy our ranks in this house a man who had given long years of public service in many fields. On behalf of the party I have the honour to lead I join with the Prime Minister in expressing our profound sympathy to the members of Mr. Noseworthy's family in his untimely death. I also extend to his associates in the party to which he gave such devoted service our sympathy in their loss.

maintopic: THE LATE J. W. NOSEWORTHY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to be associated with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in paying tribute to our late colleague, Mr. Noseworthy. When I contemplate the empty seat beside me which formerly was occupied by Mr. Noseworthy, and when I think of my own recent experience, I cannot help noting the appalling way in which heart disease is taking its toll of the Canadian people, and all too frequently of the members of this house. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that under the circumstances we ought to be redoubling our efforts to find out the cause of this appalling loss of life and impairment of health being caused by Canada's No. 1 killer. Perhaps no greater tribute could be paid to Mr. Noseworthy than to set up some sort of memorial fund for the study of heart disease because that is the thing which, if not directly certainly indirectly, took his life.
I want to pay my tribute to Mr. Nose worthy as a sincere and kindly gentleman whom I always enjoyed meeting and who always treated me very well. He was a fighter for the betterment of those people who most need help in our country, and he was always working on their behalf.
I want to join with the others in extending my sympathy to the members of his family in their irreparable loss and also to extend to the leader of the C.C.F. party and his colleagues our sympathy in their loss of a devoted colleague.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, would you allow me to express to you and to the members of the house my sincere thanks and gratitude for the warm welcome extended to me today. May I tell you how happy I am to be back in my place in the House of Commons. I have always felt that the greatest blessing that can come to any man is to be able to work all his days. I am glad to say that my doctors have given me encouragement. They say that it will be possible for me now to ease into the work gradually, and I hope I shall be able to take my full responsibility before long.
During the time I was in hospital in Calgary I received thousands of messages of encouragement, understanding and good will IMr. Drew.]

from people all across Canada. Amongst those were many from this house and from my colleagues here. Those messages gave me great encouragement and a lift that was much like a transfusion. They contributed in no mean way to the speed with which I was able to recover. I want to thank all hon. members for their kindness to me and for the kindness they have extended to my family while I was absent and impaired. I am glad to be back and wish to express my sincere thanks to all.

maintopic: THE LATE J. W. NOSEWORTHY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first express my appreciation for the kindly references that have been made to the party which I have the honour to lead in this house in the loss that we have sustained in the death of a good friend and colleague. Joe Noseworthy's life was devoted to good causes throughout the whole of it. As the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said, he was born under humble circumstances in a fisherman's home in Newfoundland. He literally had to fight his way through school. Then he devoted his life for some time to the Grenfell mission in Labrador where he worked for the health and the welfare of the people of that part of Newfoundland which is now also a part of this country.
He came to Canada in 1910, making up his mind that he would complete his university course. He worked his way through university by taking all kinds of work in the summer to enable him to get through. There he specialized in English and in history, becoming later on, as the Prime Minister has said, a teacher in one of the Ontario high schools where he remained for a number of years, indeed until he was elected as a member of the House of Commons. May I just say in passing that one of the assets he had when he was seeking election to this house in 1942 was that he had made great friends of the students of Vaughan collegiate where he was a teacher, and they wholeheartedly went out to support him in that election, a fact which I think was a great tribute to him as a teacher and friend of the young people in that community.
I knew him long before he came to this house. When I was the president of the Canadian Teachers' Federation he was associated with the secondary school teachers of Ontario. He contributed greatly to the welfare of the teaching profession of this country. The excellent brief which was presented to the Rowell-Sirois commission when it sat in this city some years ago was largely the work of the late Joseph Noseworthy, and the teachers of the country are grateful to him and appreciative of the work that he did for them in that regard.

He was elected to this parliament in 1942. As the Leader of the Opposition, the Prime Minister and the leader of the Social Credit party have said, in this house we found him to be a great friend, a great representative of his constituency and a fine personality. We shall miss him from this place. To his colleagues and to myself, he was always a loyal friend. I feel personally that in the passing of Joseph Noseworthy I have lost one with whom I have been associated for some 30 years in the teaching profession and the House of Commons, and that is a very real and personal loss as well as a loss to the party which I represent.
We too join in expressing our deepest sympathy to his widow, his daughters, his son and other members of the family in their sad and sudden bereavement.
Sometimes we can find in the literature of our language something which appropriately describes an individual. Robert Browning, in one of his poems, wrote these words:
One who never turned his back but marched breast forward,
Never doubted clouds would break,
Never dreamed, though right were worsted, wrong would triumph,
Held we fall to rise, are baffled to fight better, Sleep to wake.
I know of no words more appropriate than those to describe the life and work of Joseph Noseworthy.

maintopic: THE LATE J. W. NOSEWORTHY
speechtext: I should like to say a brief word, Mr. Speaker. Because our colleague belonged to the same branch of the church as I do, I felt it was my duty, as well as my privilege, to call on him when he was ill. I was cheered because I found he was not afraid of death, and what we know as death was to him a release to a greater life and larger liberty: not dead but living.

speechtext:
I wish to make a statement concerning the transport of supplies out of Eagle, Alaska, in connection with the construction by the United States of the distant early warning line.
The agreement between Canada and the United States for the construction of the D.E.W. line in Canada provides that Canadian carriers will to the fullest extent practicable be afforded the opportunity to participate in D.E.W. 'line transportation in Canada; and as hon. members know, the greater part of the airlift for the D.E.W. line has been carried out by Canadian air carriers. The transport of 67509-173i
National Defence-D.E.W. line construction materials to D.E.W. line sites offers many difficulties and has necessitated the use of different routes and different modes of transportation.
During the winter of 1954-55 Alaska Freight Lines-a United States company which operates barges between Seattle and Alaska and trucks and tractors in Alaska, and which has, I understand, a Canadian subsidiary-moved certain materials for the D.E.W. line by means of a snow train from Circle, Alaska, almost due north to Shingle Point on the Arctic coast in the Yukon. From there it hauled the freight eastward along the coast to certain D.E.W. line sites in Canada.
During the summer of 1955 information from United States sources indicated that it was expected that the same facilities would be used in the winter of 1955-1956 over the same route between Circle and Shingle Point. After examining the matter, the Canadian authorities were satisfied that these snow-train services out of Alaska would be needed during the winter of 1955-1956 for the purpose of the construction of the D.E.W. line. Failure to move the material would have resulted in a serious delay in the shipments urgently required for the D.E.W. line work this winter, but it was pointed out to the United States authorities that any extensive and continuing use of snow trains in Canada should be based upon the use of Canadian operators. I am informed that at least one Canadian company was approached by the construction contractor in that sector, but that company indicated that it could not be ready in time for operations this winter. This is not surprising because not only are considerable organization and extensive equipment necessary, but the route northward from Circle, Alaska, is not in an area in which Canadian operators are normally interested.
In developing its plans for operations in the winter of 1955-56, Alaska Freight Lines found it desirable to cut a winter road from Eagle, Alaska, eastward to Norman Wells and thence northeastward to the Arctic coast. This change of route was made without consultation with the Canadian government, and accordingly final permission for the operation was withheld by the Canadian authorities until the company had supplied full details as to the operation and had satisfied Canadian officials that it would comply with all applicable Canadian laws and regulations.
May I now, Mr. Speaker, deal with the subject of complaints. A joint complaint from two Canadian charter air carriers, one at Whitehorse and the other at Dawson, alleging that Alaska Freight Lines was improperly using United States aircraft to assist the snow-train operations in Canadian territory,

Proposed Legislation
was received by the air transport board. Upon investigation it was found that though Alaska Freight Lines may, in its earlier operations to which I have referred, have made use of United States aircraft, it was, at the time of the complaint, using the services of one Canadian and one United States light aircraft.
No other complaint has been received by the departments of national defence, transport and national revenue.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that what I have just said replies fully to the question which the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) addressed to the Prime Minister on the orders of the day on March 23.
I understand that the Whitehorse board of trade did prepare a brief criticizing the operations in Canadian territory of Alaska Freight Lines and suggesting that it was not conforming with Canadian laws and regulations. This brief was addressed not to the government but to the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Simmons), who communicated its contents to the departments concerned. These departments report that the laws and regulations administered by them have been complied with and that the necessary steps have been taken to ensure that they will continue to be complied with. The hon. member for Yukon has informed me that the principal object which the Whitehorse board of trade had in mind was the operations next winter, 1956-57, and I hope that it will be possible to satisfy them on this point.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the Prime Minister if he will inform the hon. members of this house in regard to what was discussed, and, in so far as that is possible, what was achieved at the meeting in Virginia which he attended just before Easter.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PUBLIC SERVICE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON VISIT OF PRIME MINISTER WITH PRESIDENT OF UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I anticipated that there might be such a question and I prepared a rather brief statement of what took place there which otherwise I would not have inflicted upon the house ten or twelve days after the visit that has been so fully, although

not always as accurately as fully, reported in the newspapers of both countries.
This visit took place at White Sulphur Springs on March 26 and 27 between the heads of governments of the United States, Mexico and Canada. The host at this meeting was the President of the United States who in his invitation and subsequently emphasized that it would be of an informal character without agenda for the purpose of exchanging views on matters of mutual interest and of getting to know each other better.
In view of the character of the meeting, no decisions were reached and none was expected. It was, however, from my point of view, both helpful and agreeable to be in a position to discuss current international affairs with the presidents of the United States and Mexico in this informal way. There was also an opportunity to bring up one or two subjects of specific Canadian-United States concern with President Eisenhower and Mr. Dulles.
The general discussion centred largely upon the comprehensive report which Mr. Dulles made on his recent visit to Asia. It has been stated in the press that in the subsequent exchange of views there was an emphatic expression of policy difference between the United States and Canada in respect of communist China. The reports in that form are without foundation. It is quite true that both President Eisenhower and Mr. Dulles explained very frankly the reasons why recognition of the communist government at Peking could not be contemplated under present circumstances and why they felt their support should be continued to the government of Chiang Kai-shek. However, there was nothing said about the Canadian position which would suggest any change whatsoever from that stated in the house by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) on January 31 either in respect of recognition or of our attitude toward the islands of Quemoy and Matsu off the coast of China.
Each government is fully aware of the position of the other in these matters, as indeed they were before the meeting at White Sulphur Springs. It is true, however, and this was recognized at our recent meeting, that there are many countries which have recognized the Peking regime, and that this has created a problem as to which regime should represent China at the United Nations, a problem which may be expected to grow more acute as time goes on.
There was considerable discussion over the position in the Middle East, the seriousness of which, of course, everyone recognized. It was agreed that, while all possible steps to
Inquiries of the Ministry reduce immediate tension should be taken, peace could only be secured there by an agreed political settlement between Israel and its neighbours. In this connection, the three governments welcomed the expected intervention of the United Nations at this time, since formalized through the resolution which has just been passed unanimously by the security council. I am sure that the Secretary General of the United Nations has our best wishes for success in the very important mission on which he is now engaged in consequence of this resolution.
There was also general discussion of the possible consequences of recent communist party developments in Russia. I got the impression that it was felt that any firm conclusion in regard to the long-range importance of these changes would be premature but that, in any event, they would not warrant any relaxation of effort on our part, either in defence or diplomacy or negotiation.
Consideration was also given to the problems arising out of the emergence of new states in Asia and Africa, states which are as sensitive about their national independence as they are insistent on greater human welfare for their people. In this connection there was an exchange of views as to the desirability of continuing international economic assistance to materially underdeveloped countries, and especially as to the importance of removing any feeling that such assistance on the part of western countries had any ulterior motive or was inspired by any other spirit than good will and understanding. On the Canadian side, we expressed the view that it might help to remove any suspicions of ulterior motives if the United Nations were brought more into the picture than it had been, at least from the point of view of using the organization as a clearing house for plans and policies and information in regard to international assistance schemes. We felt that this had been done with good results in the annual meetings of the ministerial committee of the Colombo plan, and that possibly this practice could be usefully extended to the wider field of the United Nations, so that it would become clear to the whole world community what various countries were doing in this matter and why they were doing it.
In our bilateral talks, I emphasized once again to the President the importance of better-balanced trade between our two countries. I referred to the existing unfavourable balance in our visible trade, and I mentioned that the compensation or correction of this imbalance by capital movements occasionally was the cause of some concern in this country

Inquiries of the Ministry lest the control of our economic development, which should remain in Canadian hands, might be prejudiced thereby.
I also suggested to the President that the time seemed to have come when problems regarding the use of water power on rivers crossing the international boundary might well be studied at a conference between representatives of the two governments. Here I might perhaps extend this a little to answer a question of which notice was telephoned to my office by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). There was no discussion of the problem, but merely the suggestion that it would probably be desirable at this time to have it studied by a joint conference representing the two governments, to try to get at something which would make for the possibility of expeditious use of these water powers to the best possible advantage of the people who might derive advantage from their use. It was left at that, with the understanding that the subject would be further pursued in discussions between our Department of External Affairs and the Secretary of State of the United States.
Needless to say, the President expressed a very warm feeling for this country and gratification at the way in which relations between our two peoples were based on mutual respect and friendship and frank statement of diverging views, when there were diverging views. He took advantage of the opportunity to mention some concern over the proposed 20 per cent advertising tax on Canadian editions of United States magazines. My explanation to him of the nature and purpose of this proposal will serve, I hope, to lessen his concern about it.
Having to make this statement, I would not want to end it without expressing once again my grateful thanks to the President and the government of the United States for the kindness and friendly hospitality which they showed us during our visit. I would also like to express my sincere appreciation of the opportunity thus afforded to me to become acquainted with the President of Mexico and to renew my acquaintance with the foreign minister of Mexico. It should be a source of real gratification to all Canadians that the relations between Canada and Mexico are developing in such an important and satisfactory way.

Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). My election was also, in large measure, a tribute on the part of the electorate to the innumerable and important services rendered to them over the years by my father and predecessor, Senator the Hon. C. G. Power, in whose eminent footsteps I hope to prove a worthy follower. The tradition which he has left me is one of unstinting and devoted service in the interests of the electors of Quebec South, of the city and province of Quebec and of Canada. It is also a tradition of party loyalty and service tempered with clearness and independence of thought. Indeed, it is a tradition which he continues to maintain in his new legislative function, and which I will also endeavour, to the best of my ability, to continue in and out of this house.
And now, Mr. Speaker, I crave your kind indulgence while I say a few brief words about the constituency which I have the honour of representing here and while I discuss certain problems of local interest.
The constituency of Quebec South comprises generally speaking that part of the city of Quebec where the Palais station, the harbour, the Battlefields park, the walled town and upper town are located. It also includes the. city of Sillery which is undergoing a rapid growth. Within its limits is to be', "The Budget-Mr. F. G. Power found the first permanent European settlement in Canada. It has felt the tread of the most illustrious figures of Canadian history: Champlain, Maisonneuve,-whose house in Sillery still stands today-Frontenac, Laval, Montcalm and Wolfe, Cartier, Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier, to name but a few. The riding has been the site of the capital of French Canada and of the United Provinces of Canada. The Quebec conference preceding confederation was held there. And within its limits are to be found the provincial parliament buildings. In brief, my constituency is the birthplace of Canada and of Quebec.
While I am on that subject, Mr. Speaker, I would like to suggest to the government that because of the historical importance of that city and consequently of the attraction it has for Canadians and Americans, consideration might be given to some financial assistance to the municipality in the form of subsidies or otherwise, especially if we take into account the value of untaxed crown property in the city. In this way the municipal government would be in a position to discharge its heavy responsibilities and to increase the beauty and attractiveness of the city.
But the constituency of Quebec South has more than a historical interest. It also is part of modern Quebec whose progress since 1941 has been truly marvellous. Quebec offers unique advantages from the point of view of the establishment of new industries.
Quebec is one of the main shoe manufacturing districts in Canada. There you find more than 500 industries including bookbinding, tobacco, cigar and cigarettes, ladies' wear, agricultural products, food, furs, iron works, breweries, clothing, wood, pulp and paper.
The town of Sillery which is going to commemorate this year, between the 2nd and the 11th of June, the centenary of the incorporation of its municipality and of its school board, is a pleasant residential town which has grown rapidly since 1945 and of which my forefathers have been among the first settlers.
Now I would like to say a few words relating to some problems with which we are particularly concerned. One of the most important factors in the economic life of my constituency and of the city and district of Quebec is the harbour of Quebec.
The harbour of Quebec, as well as those of Halifax, Saint John, Chicoutimi, Montreal,
fMr. Power (Quebec South).]", "Three Rivers, Churchill and Vancouver, is administered by the national harbours board, an institution which was established under chapter 42 of the Statutes of Canada for the year 1936.
Before the adoption of this legislation, the harbour of Quebec was state property and was administered by three government officials called the Quebec harbour commission. The change in the administration was made following Sir Alexander Gibb's recommendations, which he formulated after carrying on, at the request of the government, an inquiry into Canada's national harbours. His conclusions' were to the effect that the administrative system used was not satisfactory.
Consequently, the setting up of a central authority was proposed in order to co-ordinate direction and to supervise finance and works of a technical nature. Besides the central authority, the recommendation was also made to substitute for the harbour commissioners a local civil servant who would be called port manager. This official would have the direction of each harbour under the central authority. The National Harbours Board Act, chapter 42, statutes of 1936, gave effect to the above proposals.
Another recommendation, subordinate to the one above but which, unfortunately, was not put into effect, called for the setting up of a local harbour board which was to represent local interests and those that used the harbour, and would also help out the harbour master in matters of purely local concern.
The partial implementation of the Gibb report, as I have just indicated, resulted in a centralization which evoked almost unanimous criticism throughout the country, criticism which took the form of speeches and resolutions recorded from time to time in the orders of the day of this house.
The policy implemented as a result of the very nature of this act administered by the national harbours board has prevented the adoption of any corrective measure which could have been brought forward so as to stimulate the export of goods through the port of Quebec.
Consequently, Quebec harbour, though showing a balance sheet which is favourable in appearance, is not as widely used and known as it should be. We must not forget that the Quebec harbour commissioners did much to attract business to Quebec and that they fought to obtain concessions such as the preferential tariff on grain carried from Fort William to Quebec on the national transcontinental railway in 1921 and 1926. Since the disappearance of this harbour commission,", "its functions of promoting trade in Quebec city have, to a certain extent, been assumed by the Quebec city chamber of commerce. Be that as it may, promotion carried out by that organization is obviously not as wide in scope as it would be if it were carried out by an authority having direct connections with the harbour.
The inherent weakness of the National Harbours Board Act as' it now stands is to be found in the fact that it is not within the terms of reference of the board, nor even of the local port manager, to promote competition between harbours. With regard to Quebec, it would seem that the harbour authorities are completely indifferent to any encouragement or stimulation of local business or to promotion or growth of regional and foreign trade. Indeed, the material assets of Quebec harbour have been so sadly neglected that they have deteriorated in an alarming way. Yet, recently, and as a result of representations made by the chamber of commerce, and supported by all federal members for that area in this house, an impressive program of reconstruction and improvements has been launched and it appears that, following instructions by the government, the national harbour board intends to recondition Quebec harbour. Though such action would be of great help, it would not be enough to ensure the prosperity of this port. It is essential that the recommendations of the Gibb report which I mentioned before, and which have not yet been passed-or some similar legislation-be added to the act so as to improve our domestic and foreign trade and to promote the development of the city by giving the harbour administration a more complete autonomy in co-operation with local business, industrial and labour interests.

Mr. Speaker, there are two points which I would like to discuss, first as the member


for St. Mary, and also simply as a representative from the province of Quebec. My hon. friend, the member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand), recently mentioned a subject which deserves the particular attention of the federal authorities; I mean the rubberized footwear industry in our province. I think it is my duty to stress the point with the greatest firmness, because in my own riding the Dominion Rubber Company is operating a plant which, according to its management, is unfortunately bound to close down if competition due to the importation of those foreign and commonwealth products continues to increase.
Like several other members of this house, I received from the management a brief on the position of this particular industry, and I think I should insist and draw to the attention of the house certain figures which will doubtlessly give some food for thought to those whose responsibility it is to look after our trade balance. I would moreover draw the government's attention to the necessity of reviewing our policy with regard to the importation of certain goods, which is proving very damaging to the industry I just mentioned.
The hon. member for Terrebonne described the position very clearly, and I commend him for doing so. It is indeed not the first time that we benefit from his experience; he is one of those who are concerned with all questions of vital interest to our country. Of course, he also more especially looks after the interests of his own county.
The Dominion Rubber Company also operates a factory in the county of Terrebonne, and the employees risk losing their jobs because of the conditions he has so well described and on which I would like to comment for a moment. Because of a preferential trade agreement which goes back to 1932, I believe, at which time the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was prime minister of this country, certain commonwealth industrialists, such as those in Hong Kong, were allowed to take advantage of our preferential tariff and to export certain goods to this country, notably rubberized footwear. I definitely share the view of those who say that this treaty is out of date. Not only is it out of date as far as that industry is concerned, but perhaps also in other cases as well.
In 1949, for instance, we imported 2,000 pairs of rubberized footwear, while in 1954 this figure had risen to one million pairs imported from various places such as Hong Kong.

For the ten first months of the year 1955, 2,186,928 pairs of rubberized footwear were imported from various places. These figures immediately show the seriousness of the competition with which our local industry is faced.
But that is not all. We must remember that, in that same period, our exports were substantially reduced, since we are in no position to compete with a market like Hong Kong's for instance, where workers are paid about 10 cents an hour, whereas the average hourly wage of a Canadian worker is about $1.45. We can therefore not expect to export this product to Europe or elsewhere since we cannot meet the competition of such cheap labour. To my mind the main factor in the price differential is not the cost of the material, but rather the labour costs. Until 1949 we were able to manufacture these products very profitably, but at this time competition has become highly dangerous and threatens to snuff out the local market.
I am no expert on the matter, Mr. Speaker, but it does seem to me that a thirty-two year old treaty should be revised. To my mind, not only should the suggestion made by the hon. member for Terrebonne be given serious consideration, but import quotas should be established. As the hon. member for Terrebonne so aptly stated, such an attitude would allow the canvas and rubber shoe industry to stabilize its situation, to see where it is going, because the leaders of this industry are really alarmed. In fact, judging from the brief they submitted to us, they do not beat around the bush about it. To them, the situation is so critical that they summarize this report by stating that there are only three alternatives. Either go out of business completely, or else import these products themselves and resell them, taking into account the very low price at which they could secure them from abroad because of the extremely lower level of salaries paid in these countries exporting canvas and rubber shoes, as I pointed out a while ago. Or else, they could close down in this country and set themselves in business in those countries where they could obtain labour at rates of 8 to 10 cents an hour.
So, Mr. Speaker, I thought it a good thing to add my humble observations to those of the hon. member for Terrebonne. If I did not speak at length on this subject, it was because it was dealt with in a masterly way by my hon. friend, but I think it my duty to insist in order that the government consider
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis this matter seriously and help the canvas and rubber shoe industry of this country.
Now, the second point I should like to deal with, in the time left at my disposal is one of local interest and one which I bring up at each session. It is the matter of toll bridges. Many a subject has been often discussed in this house, and by raising them repeatedly their sponsors finally reached their goals. I wish that the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) would listen to, or read if he is not here, the few remarks I have to make on this subject.
This is not just a purely local matter. If I bring it up it is not because the bridge begins or ends-according to where you come from, in my riding. Nevertheless, I believe that this discussion will help set a pattern all across Canada as far as toll bridges are concerned, if they continue to exist.
According to the request of an association in my riding, I wish to suggest that the tolls be made uniform. If they cannot be made uniform in all provinces, I suggest then that they should be standardized at least in the same province, or, as far as I am concerned, in the province of Quebec, at the very least.
To my mind, Mr. Speaker, tolls should be charged on cars only, and not on passengers, if it is indeed necessary to maintain these tolls, which-I cannot emphasize that too strongly-I still find very hard to understand.
Is my time nearly over, Mr. Speaker? Well, you have to make allowance for the fact that I was interrupted for a few minutes.
So I would suggest that tolls be uniform. Then, as far as Jacques Cartier bridge is concerned, I think that the toll-gates should be on the south shore so that the people of Montreal could get to Ste. Helene island- which belongs to the city of Montreal-without paying the toll. I never heard in any city, in any country, that a citizen had to pay a toll to cross a bridge in his own city. I have seen citizens pay something to cross over to another country, to another city or to another province, but I have never seen any place where a citizen had to pay a toll to get to his own property. If the collection booths were moved to the south side, my fellow citizens could, go to Ste. Helene island where the city of Montreal has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to turn it into a most attractive public park. I feel that the national harbours board which administers the bridge should grant all the citizens of Montreal the privilege of travelling free of charge to their

The Budget-Mr. Hees own property on Ste. Helene island! which, as I said a moment ago, has been improved to the cost of hundreds of thousands of dollars by the city of Montreal which, in the past, has largely contributed to the payment of the Jacques Cartier bridge deficits. Now that the bridge brings in considerable revenues, it should be obvious that any citizen of Montreal must be given at least the privilege of going around within his own city without having to pay for moving from one street to another or from one side of the river to the other.
I have made these two suggestions. I shall come back to this same subject anyway when the estimates of the Department of Transport are called. I regret not to have more time at my disposal to explain the many reasons why tolls on those bridges should be abolished. However, if this cannot be done, let there be a toll for vehicles only and not for passengers; let there be a standard rate for all bridges so that tickets may be used anywhere, at least within a province, and so that the citizens of Montreal may go to Ste. Helene island without having to pay for using a bridge for which the city of Montreal has contributed hundreds of thousands of dollars.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in travelling around the country and talking to one's constituents and people in other parts of the country, the first thing that strikes one is the intense disappointment on the part of the people in the budget which the government brought down three weeks ago. People consider this is a cynical, political budget, brought in for one purpose and one purpose only, namely, to provide a kind of psychological buildup which this government obviously believes is necessary as a curtain-raiser to next year's election budget. There are no tax reductions this year. There will be small tax reductions, or perhaps reasonably large tax reductions, next year. People will feel happy and the government hopes they will go to the polls and vote Liberal. This is nothing more or less than a straight political budget. Tax reductions could have been made easily, and the government is very much to be criticized, and is being very severely criticized by people from one end of the country to the other, for indulging in no more nor less than a cynical political budget at this time.
What this country needs, Mr. Speaker, among many other things, is the introduction


of budgetary measures which will create an economic atmosphere which will induce a far more rapid industrial expansion in this country than we are having at the present time or have had for many years past.
The United Nations statistical bureau issued figures in January which showed that the rate of industrial expansion in Canada has been far slower than that of any of our main industrial competitors. By refusing to introduce measures which will correct this sorry state of affairs the government is making it very clear that it is perfectly willing for Canada to continue to be primarily a producer of raw materials, to feed the machines of the United States and of other industrial countries.
Of course, these countries are delighted to use our raw materials to create profits for their industries and employment for their people. They find it very hard to understand why a country like Canada should be so willing to go on making its raw materials available to them and allowing them to have the profits and greater employment while we seem to be quite content to accept the lesser end of the bargain. However, of course, they say, "if you are willing to go on doing that it suits our purpose very well, but we cannot understand why you are willing to do it."
The government's latest move to help United States industry is its proposal to use public funds to enable United States interests to take over the control of the transportation and marketing of a large proportion of one of our most important natural resources, namely, natural gas. This action has mobilized Canadian public opinion as perhaps nothing else could have done, and it has made us realize that for some time past we have been handing over more and more of our resources to the people of the United States. When the people of Canada see the government using public funds to accelerate this process it makes them realize to what extraordinary lengths this process has gone and the degree to which this government has fallen under the domination of United States financial interests. Unless this present process is stopped, Canadians are going to become merely economic vassals of the United States, supplying their factories with raw materials and their people with jobs.
A further example of the government allowing Americans to move in and take over control of operations which should be handled by Canadians was the information which we received a few weeks ago that a United States contractor is to have the control and operation of our distant early warning radar line. We have in our armed forces the

technical personnel necessary to handle this operation. Any shortage in training at the moment could be made up within a period of three months. The government's action in handing over control of the operations of our D.E.W. line is simply further evidence of this government's supine submission to United States pressure.
What is happening is that we have been selling more and more of the ownership of our enterprises to attempt to balance our current account deficit with the United States. Recently, the dominion bureau of statistics published figures which show that during the past year this was the principal means we used to try to balance our record $665 million current account deficit with the United States.
This sort of thing must stop, Mr. Speaker, and the first step we should take is to balance our current account with the United States. The best way to do that is to start manufacturing here in Canada many more of the manufactured articles which we are buying at the present time from that country. For some unexplained reason we seem to be perfectly content, as I said a few minutes ago, to ship most of our primary products to the United States and other industrial countries, and then buy back much of this raw material in its finished form.
By exporting our resources in their raw state, we are simply taking the easy way to make a dollar instead of making $4 or $5 or more by carrying our manufacturing process through to its conclusion here in Canada. For every hour of employment which we gain by exporting our resources in their raw state, we would gain many hours of employment by carrying production through to its finished stage.
The new plants that would be required to make this possible are going to be built only if industries become convinced that it is to their advantage to manufacture in Canada. The most important factor, of course, is cost of production. We must show potential industry that their cost of production will be lower in order to attract them to establish plants here and start manufacturing. In the past, ambitious and alert municipalities have offered potential industry all sorts of concessions to attract them to their locality. These concessions have included such things as free grants of land, cheap water and hydro rates, reduced taxes for an initial period, and the provision of roads, docks, sidings and other necessary transportation facilities. These municipalities have been repaid many times over in the form of increased employment and trade, and the taxes that accrue from both.
I believe that such a program to attract potential industry to all parts of Canada should be pursued with system and vigour
The Budget-Mr. Hees from one end of this country to the other. To see that this is done I believe there should be established in Canada a Canadian industrial development board composed of topflight personnel who would work with the provinces, and through them with the municipalities, in order to find out what concessions could be made to potential industry. With that information available, the board could act as a clearing house and could approach potential industry in order that as much industry as possible, in the shortest possible time, could be established in this country.
An industrial development board such as I envisage would work with provincial governments and through them with municipal governments to explore all possible concessions which these bodies would be willing to make in order to attract industry to their areas. This board would also work with transportation companies to find out what transportation facilities in the way of docks and railway sidings and the like they would be willing to provide for the extra business which would result from the establishment of new plants in the various localities.
If a program of this kind is pursued with imagination and vigour it will greatly assist us in setting in motion a rate of industrial expansion which can equal or exceed that of our industrial competitors. If they can reach the rate of expansion they have reached, there is no reason in the world why a country such as Canada with its tremendous wealth of power and natural resources cannot have as great or a greater rate of industrial expansion.
In addition to the concessions which the provincial and municipal governments could be persuaded to offer, concessions which I believe will be paid back many times over in the form of increased employment and trade, and tax revenues which will accrue from both, the federal government can also offer inducements in eight forms.
First of all it could offer a graduated corporation income tax spread over the period it is estimated a new industry requires to get on its feet. If, for example, such a period is estimated to be 15 years, the tax for the first year would be one-fifteenth of the normal rate and would increase steadily until after 15 years the company would be paying the full rate. The important thing is that there would be no loss to the government by the introduction of such a program because these new industries do not exist at the present time and of course they are not paying taxes. I believe they will not exist unless the federal, provincial and municipal governments are willing to make concessions which will persuade industries that it is to
2736	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Hees their advantage to process in Canada. After this is done, the Canadian government will benefit from those taxes, but until those industries are induced to establish plants here, there will be no industries and no taxes. In making a concession of this kind, therefore, the federal government would be losing nothing in the form of taxes, but would gain by the ultimate taxes which would result from such a move.
Secondly, the government can make a material reduction in its sales and excise taxes without loss of tax revenue. By lowering sales and excise taxes the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) would be making it possible to lower the selling price of many of our products which are today being priced out of the market. By helping our products to become more competitive, the minister would be stimulating sales, and these increased sales multiplied by a lower unit tax, may very easily equal or exceed our present tax totals.
An example was given to the minister during the past year of just how true this can be. In his previous budget, after considerable pressure had been brought to bear upon him by the automotive industry and the official opposition, he reduced the excise tax on automobiles from 15 per cent to 10 per cent. He estimated in his budget-the budget before last-that this would cost him a considerable amount in loss of tax revenue, but the actual result was that lower prices, made possible by the lower tax, greatly stimulated sales and taxes as well. An increased number of car sales, multiplied by the lower excise tax, resulted in an increase of $8 million in excise taxes paid on new automobiles.
The third thing that the government can do is to reduce today's high income tax. Again I believe that this can be done without loss of tax revenue, because by reducing income taxes the minister is simply going to make it possible for more people to spend more of their incomes on the things they need. That would make it possible for more goods and services to be sold, and more people would become employed producing these additional goods and services. They will be paying income taxes instead of drawing on the government for unemployment insurance or direct relief. There would also be many additional products carrying sales and excise taxes in the future.
Fourthly, I believe that the government can encourage small industries to expand and become big industries by introducing a graduated corporation tax on corporation incomes between $20,000 and, say, $50,000 a year. At the present time a corporation pays 20 per cent on an income of up to $20,000 a year, and on the next $1,000 of income it pays 47 per cent. This provides very little inducement


to expand to a firm that is doing a comfortable business of $20,000 a year and paying a 20 per cent tax, because as soon as it does so, half of its additional income is taken in taxes. If the rate of increase between $20,000 and $50,000 a year is graduated, many industries that are small industries today will be induced to enlarge and take on the added responsibilities and worries which go with an industrial expansion.
Any initial tax losses which the government will experience, I believe, will be more than made up in the very near future by the additional sales, excise, and income taxes, which will accrue from the additional sales and employment resulting from the expansion which such a measure will induce.
Fifthly, the government can help to improve the competitive position of industry through enabling industry to undertake a greatly expanded research program, if the minister will allow a more reasonable tax write-off for expenditures made on research. At the present time the government allows only five per cent of the taxable income of the previous year, unless special permission is obtained from the minister. That means that a company which wishes to undertake a research program that will cost in excess of five per cent of the income of the previous year must wait until approximately half the current year is over, and then the decision of the Minister of National Revenue may be an unfavourable one. As any businessman knows, a decision to undertake a research program must be made well in advance of the beginning of the year, and cannot wait until the previous year's figures have been first audited and then given to the Department of National Revenue for that department to put the figures through its usual procedure of red tape.
Another factor which militates against undertaking an expanded research program at the present time is that expanded research is most needed after a bad year, when the amount allowable for tax deductions would be least. This points up the present unreality of the government's approach to the need for expanded research in this country at the present time. In Great Britain, a company is allowed to write off completely all expenses-both current expenses and capital expenses-that it undertakes for research purposes, and I believe that this government would do well to follow the same plan. I do not think that it will suffer any tax loss by so doing, because the increased employment and sales that would be made possible through additional research and the taxes they will carry in the future would more than make up for any initial tax loss which the government might suffer.

Sixthly, the government could help new industry through an accelerated depreciation program, which would permit new industries to write off their investment far more quickly than they do at the present time. This would not cost the government one penny when it is spread over the present depreciation period.
Seventhly, the government could assist gas and oil companies materially by allowing them a more generous depletion allowance on oil and gas wells. This would greatly encourage exploration and development, and would put them on a basis more comparable with their United States competitors. At the present time the United States allows a depletion allowance of 27J per cent of gross income, not to exceed 50 per cent of net income. This policy has encouraged the United States oil and gas companies to undertake very important exploration and development programs, with extremely beneficial results to the industry. I believe that this government would do well to adopt a similarly generous program for Canadian oil and gas companies.
Finally, I believe that the government should introduce a policy on public investment to assist the provinces to develop their power and other natural resources. It is public investment of this kind that is needed to help stimulate the private investment which we need to speed our economic expansion, which today is lagging so far behind that of our competitors. It is on the firm basis of seaways, highways, natural gas, electric power, irrigation and reclamation, that people build homes and offices and factories. If the people of Canada will lend their government $12 billion to shoot up in smoke, as they did during the second world war, surely they will lend it a billion dollars or so to be invested in self-liquidating public works which will make possible more jobs and higher more stable, tax revenues.
Now I should like to deal briefly with the 20 per cent tax that has been imposed by this government on Canadian advertising sold by United States periodicals that publish Canadian editions.

speechtext:
All advertising. First of all, why was this tax imposed? It certainly was not imposed at the request of any Canadian publication. They know perfectly well that this measure will not reduce by a single copy the number of United States periodicals sold in Canada. People are going to go on buying these American magazines because they provide a type of presentation of news and views which is not provided by any Canadian publication at the present time. They are going
The Budget-Mr. Hees to continue to buy these magazines until comparable publications are produced in Canada.
This tax, Mr. Speaker, is nothing more or less than a punitive tax imposed for a purely political reason. That reason is that the government has been severely embarrassed by the widespread criticism it has so justly received because of its willingness to use public funds to make easier the acquisition of Canadian resources by United States interests. I believe that the imposition of this tax is nothing more than a frantic and very futile attempt to show that the government is not really as meekly submissive to United States pressure as its pipe line proposal has very clearly demonstrated it to be. Unfortunately, however, it has chosen an attempt to hinder the sale of United States publications that publish news and views not available in a similar form in Canada, as its means of doing so.
If the government wants to help Canadian publications to increase their circulation at the expense of United States periodicals, then let it adopt a positive and constructive, instead of a negative and destructive, approach to the problem. Such an approach could well take the form of a reduction in postal rates for Canadian publications. To encourage foreign publications to increase their percentage of Canadian content, the government could allow the same percentage reduction in postal rates as their Canadian content bears to the remainder of the publication. Such a measure would be easy to introduce and administer, and it would serve the dual purpose of helping Canadian publications and encouraging foreign publications to increase their percentage of Canadian content.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what about the effect that this tax has had on our relations with the United States? It is obvious that it has had a very bad effect indeed. In view of what the United States has done recently to maintain good relations by refusing to allow restrictive legislation to be passed against a Canadian company, I believe we should examine this whole measure very carefully indeed. When the senate and legislature of the state of Maryland, by overwhelming majorities in each house, passed a bill denying the Carling Brewing Company of Canada the right to build a plant in Maryland, the United States state department wrote a very strong letter to Governor Mc-Keldin urging him to veto the measure because it was felt that it would create an unfriendly attitude towards Canada. Because the bill had been passed by overwhelming majorities in both Maryland houses, it was very difficult

The Budget-Mr. Balcom for the governor to veto the measure, but in response to a personal call by the President of the United States, Governor McKel-din did so.
If the President of the United States thought that the Carling affair was of sufficient importance for him personally to ask Governor McKeldin to face the severe criticism he would have to face in his state by vetoing the measure, then surely the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) must take the maintenance of international relations as seriously, and he has no course left open to him except to reciprocate and do what the President and Secretary of State of the United States obviously requested him to do when he saw them at White Sulphur Springs, namely, withdraw this punitive and ill-considered measure.
If the Prime Minister is unwilling to do so, he will be making it very obvious that he considers the maintenance of good international relations between Canada and the United States to be merely a one-way street. I hope that he will show that he, as well as the President of the United States, is capable of taking farsighted action, and I strongly urge him to withdraw this punitive and ill-considered measure at the very earliest moment.
