speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, April 9, is the 39th anniversary of the battle of Vimy Ridge. I was reminded of it this morning when walking around the western part of the building and seeing the small inscription there. I thought we should perhaps be reminded of that great battle for it was the first battle in which the Canadian corps fought as a unit under the leadership of then Lieutenant General Sir Julian Byng. At that time some 97,000 Canadian soldiers in the corps took part in the battle. Unfortunately there were 11,297 courageous young men killed in that battle.
In speaking of Vimy Ridge I thought it might be a good opportunity to mention that we should now be thinking of a really national cenotaph, one that would do for the soldiers who have fallen in all wars. The cenotaph in Confederation square commemorating our soldiers who lost their lives in the war of 1914-18 is very good so far as that purpose is concerned, but it does not cover a broad enough field. I hope a national cenotaph will be built on parliament hill this year or next year on the site suggested by the Canadian Legion, namely, on the walk from Wellington street up to the peace tower. I think it will be a very fitting location.
I should like to be able to make a 15 minute speech but unfortunately I have many


local problems which I think should be aired in the house and brought to the attention of the various departments, the public generally and in many cases the people of Halifax. The budget speech and the accompanying papers tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) have given as usual a very complete review of the business of the nation. This year the picture is very encouraging and, indeed, there is some danger of overoptimism and inflation. It seems to me that we just get one kind of problem solved when a different one confronts us. However, we are very fortunate that they are problems with which we can cope. In other parts of the world where life is just one crisis after another there is often a great deal more at stake. We can be thankful that our economic problems are mainly those of development and distribution rather than a struggle for survival.
Speaking of distribution, may I say that we have heard a great deal both in the House of Commons and elsewhere about the problem of surpluses. Many proposals have been advanced and much advice has been offered on what should be done to dispose of our surplus apples, wheat, fish and potatoes. I think it will take something even more complicated than parity prices to provide an equitable disposal plan.
In addition to the wealth of material in the budget speech on the nation's business, there has been an abundance of information on Canada's growth and prospects presented to another august body. A spate of facts, figures and arguments has been brought out in connection with the Gordon commission. It is not only the abundance of material that is overwhelming. What is even more confusing is the strength of conviction with which diametrically opposite views on policy have been presented, backed as well by a substantial array of facts and arguments. How does the lowly politician or the ordinary voter find his way through this perplexing problem? At the risk of appearing to sermonize I am going to suggest some guide posts.
First, our human resources are our most important resources and the objectives that this suggests should be the ones we serve first. Second, we have a great Canadian heritage of both human and material resources of which we are in a sense only custodians for coming generations. Sometimes I am inclined to think that promoters imagine that Canada is a great big apple pie and that we should gorge ourselves on it.
As to human resources, I want to speak first about immigration. Immediately that one raises the subject, one is classed as being either for or against immigration. But it is not as simple as Calvin Coolidge's famous dictum on sin.

I wish it were that simple. But when you are dealing with people, things are never simple. As was pointed out in a recent statement by a labour leader, immigrants are not component parts that can be stored until needed.
A new approach is called for in respect of our immigration procedures. An excellent opportunity is now here to state clearly the objectives of our immigration policy and to set up the standards that will apply. The basic question is this: Do we want a rapidly growing population irrespective of the traditional basis of our culture? We have answered this question in part by our exclusion of certain races or rather by our obvious preference in the selection of immigrants. But it has seemed to be a negative answer rather than a positive policy.
I shall not presume to suggest the procedure that should apply but I would urge that the preservation of a Canadian nation and the democratic condition be the paramount consideration. We should recognize further that the democratic system, whatever its weaknesses, draws its vitality from the principle of the sanctity of the individual. This fact we are sometimes, I think, prone to forget. Devotion to that principle is not something learned overnight. Mere numbers are not enough to assure the preservation of a Canadian nation that represents a strong moral force in the world. We must have citizens who are prepared to accept the discipline and the responsibilities as well as the rights of a democratic society.
The case for large-scale immigration has been presented forcibly by many people. There is no doubt that Canada can and should have immigration-how much will depend on changing circumstances-and our policy should be flexible. It should vary in accordance with the best interests of both native-born citizens and prospective new immigrants. The demands for a larger labour force and a larger domestic market should be recognized but should not take priority over social considerations or concern for our absorptive capacity.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention something that I consider to be important, namely the possibility of making some reciprocal arrangement with the commonwealth countries-in particular the British isles-whereby immigrants coming to Canada might be given a shorter period in which to qualify as citizens. A man of 60 years of age who comes to this country is too old to qualify for social security. I wish arrangements could be made with the British isles and the other commonwealth countries whereby that man would receive credit for what he has paid in the old country. I think
The Budget-Mr. Balcom that is an important matter. I think we all agree that we should have more people here from the British isles. There are in my own riding several cases in which people are concerned in this problem.
On this same subject of human resources I want to quote the words of a noted economist, J. K. Galbraith, who recently appeared before the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects in support of a plea made to this house earlier this session for aid to universities and students. Mr. Galbraith said this:
Far more urgent than resource development, as just implied, is the problem of human development. It is vital that this keep abreast of the technical and scientific requirements of growth and that it stimulate growth along this dimension. Here-I speak for the United States and, I think, also for Canada-is our most serious failure. We have left the training of scientists, engineers, and highly skilled technicians largely to chance. We have suffered an enormous wastage of talent by making higher education dependent not on ability but on ability to pay. The present scramble for highly qualified people is a measure of our failure. We must plan to spend generously to correct our mistakes in this area.
I am not going to labour at this time my personal views on this matter, other than to say briefly that I firmly believe that a more generous federal policy on university finance is of vital national importance. Further, I want to emphasize the fact that it is of more than ordinary importance to Nova Scotia and the other Atlantic provinces. We are limited in the opportunities and training we can offer to our youth by our relatively small tax base. Thus in our most precious national asset, our youth, has been denied the opportunity of full development in this land flowing with honey and other sources of wealth.
We have heard with satisfaction the minister's outline of developments, past and present, which make up the picture of a booming economy with bright prospects for the future. It is important to note also that in spite of the rapid growth and spectacular changes that have taken place in our way of life, transportation and communication still remain our fundamental problems. It is natural that they should loom large in the affairs to be dealt with by parliament this session. Their garb is somewhat different from 1867, but their fundamental nature is the same. The dominant factors in the nation's business life are the enormous distances between important points and the relatively small population compared with the total land area. These are the things that dictated the formation of the publicly owned national broadcasting system, the creation of Trans-Canada Air Lines, pu,blic participation in the railway system, in the St.

The Budget-Mr. Balcom Lawrence seaway and now the proposed participation by the federal government and the province of Ontario in a gas pipe line.
A vital role in our national transportation is played by our national harbours. I want to speak particularly about the port of Halifax. I want to emphasize that the port comprises not only the waterfront of the city of Halifax and Dartmouth but also the shore of Bedford basin and the northwest arm in Halifax county. The property includes grain elevators, a cold storage plant, freight sheds, piers and all the equipment that goes with these. Great improvements have been made in these in the past number of years. In talking about the physical changes, I might mention that there has been a marked improvement in administration, better facilities and better services.
You might think these words of praise could be dismissed as those of an interested party, but I believe you will have them confirmed by those who use the port, such as ship operators and shippers, who know from experience and whose knowledge is important in determining the port of call and the direction of shipping business. Through the combined efforts of longshoremen, freight handlers, shipping companies, insurance firms and other marine service establishments, as well as the federal government, a great industry has been established. The government is to be commended for its recognition of the importance of our ports in the national interest.
Yet in spite of the increases and extensions of facilities by the national harbours board, from time to time ships are tied up in the stream waiting for space to dock. Port business would be even better if our manufactured products were shipped via Canadian ports. For example, in 1953 almost 85 per cent of the Canadian-made automobiles exported, some 37,844, were shipped via United States ports, compared with a little more than 15 per cent through Canadian ports. The picture is roughly the same in so far as farm implements and machinery exports are concerned; in the same year 80 per cent went through United States ports. In my opinion, manufacturers should be bending over to use our ports, for surely we bend backwards in giving them protection and other subsidies.
There is obviously a heavy selling job to be done if we are to attract more of the business that is going. The national harbours board has done an excellent job within the limits set by available funds. The administrative work of this board in Halifax has been assisted, supported and supplemented by the promotional work of the port of Halifax commission. The effectiveness of this organization


is indicated by the plan now under way to organize such a commission for the port of Montreal. The contribution of waterfront workers and the shipping companies has already been mentioned, but in my opinion more remains to be done.
Perhaps I need not labour the well known fact of the strategic importance of Halifax and its invaluable contribution to the defence of the free world in time of war. I think most of those in authority are well aware of that fact, but I wonder whether sufficient thought has been given to what might happen in a future catastrophe. I doubt very much whether we would have time to plan and build the additional port facilities so necessary to our survival.
I should like to make one specific suggestion as part of the long-term build-up, and that is that the national harbours board do a complete job now on pier 1-A. The plan, as I understand it, is to build about half the required length in 1956. We feel that this unit should be completed to the same length as pier B, and for various reasons. While the work is under way it would be cheaper to complete the job. Further, there is a rock pile jutting out from the centre of what will be the new pier, and this will be a hazard both for vessels coming into the new pier and vessels berthing on the north side of pier B.
While there has been steady improvement in the harbours board facilities, I cannot say that the reports are equally encouraging respecting our railway and related services. Let me say here that the Canadian National Railways have greatly improved their passenger service during the last year or so, and having done that you would imagine they would have a very forward-looking program for freight. But this does not seem to me to be the case. Halifax is served by the publicly owned Canadian National, but the management of that railway seems to take a very hard, cold look before embarking on any new developments in that area. As it is a crown corporation, decision on such matters as capital expenditures for express and freight facilities rests with the management and not with the government. The Canadian Pacific Railway does not run into Halifax, other than via the Dominion Atlantic Railway, so the incentives ordinarily provided by competition are lacking. It is quite apparent that the Canadian Pacific, as a private company, makes its own decision on whether or not it should have a line into Halifax. I cannot but wonder what the result would be if such competition existed. How much more cargo would go over Halifax piers destined for Newfoundland, for example, if there were alternative transportation?

Consider, for example, the bottleneck in cargo shipments to St. John's, Newfoundland. I have no wish to see business drawn away from North Sydney that can be properly handled on that route. However, if greater efficiency could be attained by using the existing steamship services to St. John's via Halifax, are not the residents of Newfoundland entitled to those benefits? These services via Halifax and via North Sydney should surely be complementary, not competitive. Then, too, the shortage of box cars and yardage, and the limitations of the railway facilities in Halifax have hindered the full use of the port this year.
This is hard to reconcile with the forwardlooking policies of the government in the development of national harbours board facilities. The physical facilities and the labour force were available to handle much more freight than was going through. The exports this winter, outside of wheat, have not been very good. I suppose that bottlenecks in one form or another have prevented as much going through as we would like, but I would urge upon the Minister of Transport that greater attention be given to the co-ordination of development in Halifax and Dartmouth to make the best use of what we have. If the accusation is correct that the C.N.R. is giving better service to Saint John, New Brunswick, than to Halifax, it should be investigated and the service brought in line immediately. I see the hon. member for Saint John-Albert smiling. It makes me most unhappy to think the C.N.R. would do such a thing; but it would please us even more if the railroad management adjusted traffic to the level of the importance of the respective ports.
I speak now on a different note. We are pleased at the foresight and energy that have gone into the Canadian National Steamships service to the West Indies. Because of the growing importance of the West Indies and the Caribbean area as a market for Canadian produce this is constructive public action. The traditional importance of this area to the Atlantic provinces is based on solid ground, and the economic advance that is bound to come in that area and in South America is a promising factor for future growth in the Atlantic region. We should take very positive steps in aiding this development.
In Canada glamour seems to attach to the new places, especially if they are far away from the centres of population. It seems so much easier to recognize the need for developmental expenditure in the far north, for example, than in the more settled areas of Canada. I have in mind the development of our forest potential in Halifax county and
The Budget-Mr. Balcom in eastern Nova Scotia. Several paper companies have shown interest in a site in this part of the province. A mill is now operating at Sheet Harbour which offers possibilities for further processing. Will the development division of the C.N.R. give serious study to this matter to see whether an economic proposition is hindered mainly by the lack of rail service? If that is the case, the extension of rail facilities from Musquodobit Harbour to Sheet Harbour should be thoroughly examined.
At this point perhaps I should like to say how pleased we were to read in the press information about the increase in salaries of the civil service, the navy, the army and the air force, and other branches of government. This means in the Halifax area the distribution of at least another $3 million, and I know the people of Halifax are very grateful.
There is another item I should like to mention at this time, namely the encouragement of our young people to become interested at an early age in the army, navy and air force, in the matter of enlistment or getting into the reserve. But to do this, facilities should be provided in which they can train, in which they can study and meet. I am referring to armouries in Halifax and Dartmouth. The facilities in Halifax now are inadequate, and in Dartmouth there are no such facilities. To do any training they have to go as far as eight miles, and anyone knows this is not very encouraging to people who are interested in the armed services.
Reference has been made to the St. Lawrence seaway. Great interest has been shown in this development and in its possibilities. Particularly we notice, both inside and outside the public service, great energy devoted to ways and means of keeping the waterway open in the winter. The pressure on the federal government to spend enormous sums of money on this objective will mount. Those who have a large investment in Labrador, the owners and workers in the steel mills hungry for iron ore, as well as numerous others who will use the seaway as a means of transportation will raise their voices.
It is desirable that a great national asset be used as fully as possible, but let us keep account of the cost. When we are looking at the total moneys paid out under the Maritime Freight Rates Act-this year the estimates provide for over $11 million-let us realize how very minor this is compared with the costs contemplated for ice breakers, reconnaissance planes, research and all the hidden expenses which will go into the St. Lawrence enterprise, or just that part of it pertaining to winter- navigation.

The Budget-Mr. Balcom
To refer again to the Maritime Freight Rates Act, I note with interest that the president of the C.N.R. feels, as many others do, that a close look at our transportation problems is in order. I would suggest that particular attention be paid to the Maritime Freight Rates Act, its purpose, its basis and its present achievement in relation to its objectives.
To revert to a statement made earlier, I should like to repeat my belief that we living Canadians are custodians of a great heritage. Just as important as the development of our natural resources is the need for proper conservation measures that will preserve, and indeed enhance, what we pass on to the next generations. While federal action in this field is limited to some extent by the sharing of authority with the provinces, notable steps have been taken. In forestry, jointly sponsored forest inventory work will pay off, it is to be hoped, in better forest management. Research on improved utilization of wood is making a valuable contribution to the better use of our forests. In agriculture the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act in the west and marshlands reclamation in the maritimes are adding to our capital assets. But we are really only making a beginning in this whole field.
Based on my own constituency, I can cite some situations which call for action. Along the Musquodobit river valley there is a problem of flooding which is almost perennial in the winter and spring. There must be some way in which the periodic wastage from flooding can be prevented. Some scheme of fresh water control should be feasible that would perhaps involve both agricultural and forest conservation. The particular area I speak of is located close to the large metropolitan area of Halifax and Dartmouth.
In the fisheries, good progress has been made in conservation measures to the continuing benefit of the individual fisherman as well as the whole industry. And here I should like to discuss what has become a very controversial matter in Nova Scotia, namely the protection of the inshore fisherman from the inroads of the trawlers. The Canadian law which prevents our trawlers from coming within 12 miles of the shore seems unfair to the trawler fisherman when vessels from other countries can come in to within three miles. On the other hand, it is no solution in the eyes of the inshore fisherman to let all trawlers come within three miles of shore.
The ideal solution lies in obtaining agreement among the several countries involved on a limit to which all would adhere. Theoretically we could change the law affecting our own ships, or take unilateral action to bar

foreign ships. However, we have to remember that our dealings with other countries, particularly the United States, involve a great many very important matters. One which is of vital significance to the fisheries is the United States tariff on fish products. If we should be excluded from the United States market by higher tariffs, in many parts of Nova Scotia it would not matter what was the trawler limit. It is useless to deplore our dependence on that market, for it is the place where we get a price sufficient to make it worth while for our fishermen to produce. On the other hand, this surely should not condemn us to a continuation of the present unsatisfactory regulations for much longer. I would urge the Minister of Fisheries, who understands and has discussed this situation and wishes to do something about it, to regard this question as one of very real urgency.
We have in Halifax an excellent example of international co-operation in fisheries conservation. I refer to the northwest Atlantic fisheries council with headquarters at Dal-housie University. I am sure this organization and what it represents would receive much more ardent support from the industry if we could have tangible evidence of cooperation on this matter of the trawler limit.
The budget has been described in many quarters as empty, negative and partisan. I think all three of those adjectives are ruled out if we take just one part of the budget speech and cast out all the rest. I refer to the proposed arrangements with the provinces to replace the tax rental agreements. I believe these represent a statesmanlike approach to a most difficult problem.
On the one hand the federal government must keep in mind that there is only one group of taxpayers, and whether we live in Ontario, Nova Scotia or the Yukon we must collectively provide the revenues for public services. With that in mind the total taxes collected by the dominion government, no matter how fairly they are distributed, must be kept within realistic proportions.
On the other hand the federal government has recognized the need for a certain minimum standard of Canadian services. The equalization payments will go a considerable distance in providing that minimum. At the same time, the development needs of the more rapidly growing parts of Canada must not be neglected in a share the wealth program. The federal government has shown a most commendable spirit and ingenuity in reconciling these three purposes.

Of course one cannot quarrel too much with that because if the Conservative party were on that side of the house it would have done exactly the same thing-

We should not be too surprised at this time at the kind of budget we have. It is rather difficult to pick it apart because there is nothing to pick, and the minister in making his speech on the budget did not leave very many loopholes. The minister went along very quietly in outlining the budget. When the government is in the position of throwing the shots and then sitting
The Budget-Mr. Gillis back on the defensive and allowing the opposition to carry on the war practically all by itself, it is not an easy job to criticize the budget because as long as the rules of the game are as they are, this is the way the game will be played.
I think the two groups in this corner of the house are the only groups that can make any valid criticism of the budget as it is at this time, because no one knows what we would do if we were sitting over there.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SUPPLY OF GARRY 27
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is all too true.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SUPPLY OF GARRY 27
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We might have done a much better job than the Minister of Finance did in the face of an election, but of course no one can accuse us of that because we have no record. The other two parties have records. They have established the rules of the game, and although the game has been played for a good many years the rules have not changed. The whole subject will continue to be regarded as a game until such time as the rules are changed.
I listened to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, who made practically all the criticism that could be made of the budget in the light of our amendment. It may not be a bad idea, in view of the fact that there has been a two weeks lapse of time, to put our amendment on the record again at this time as a guide to those who may read Hansard, in order that they may know to what the debate relates.
The section of the amendment that we added to the Conservative amendment reads as follows:
That the amendment be amended by inserting therein immediately after the words "United States interest" the following words:
"that it has failed to reduce the burden of sales and income taxes on those in the lower income groups, while continuing to favour privileged interests and those with unearned incomes by maintaining the 20 per cent dividend tax credit and by refusing to impose a tax on capital gains".
During the course of this session we have had several discussions on resolutions and other matters which have come before the house, which have enabled most hon. members to place their economic and financial views on record. I have taken the opportunity of doing so on a couple of occasions during the session with respect to the part of the country from which I come. At this time, however, I shall endeavour to stick as close as possible in what I have to say to the subject of the budget.
We deplore the fact that there has not been any tax relief in the low income brackets. The amendment of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made our point quite clear and I want to reiterate what he said, because I agree with him. He said that in so far as he was
2744	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Gillis concerned, if there were no tax relief given at all; if the money realized by continuing the tax structure as it is were applied to the establishment of a national health program which would bring medical aid right across the country to the hundreds of thousands of people who cannot afford any, and relieve the fear and the burden of those who may need it in the future-if the money were used for that purpose, then as far as I am concerned I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that the tax structure should remain as it is, providing the money gathered in is used for that purpose. I think that is one oi the greatest needs of this country today and one of the ways in which the average person in this country would benefit to the greatest extent.
I know that the subject of a national health program is still a controversial one in this country. I know there was not a great deal of progress made on it at the dominion-provincial conference. I know that some of the premiers, particularly in the central provinces, are still quibbling over formulas of their own, and I do not think all the people in the country understand the matter as it really is.
One of the main arguments I have heard advanced in this house, in the country and in the press particularly, over the years, is that Britain established a national health program and it does not work. It is said that it is all haywire and the doctors do not want it. That has been a line of propaganda that has been carried on all over the United States and Canada, particularly in the press, and I have heard it repeated in the house. The present British government set up a committee to make an inquiry into the administration of the national health service in Britain, as to whether it was working, whether there was waste and extravagance and whether the doctor-patient relationship had been disturbed.
Of course the present government does not believe in national health insurance to the extent that the government which established it did. When that committee was appointed, because the personnel were people who certainly were not socialists, I was of the opinion that they were appointed to try to justify the line of propaganda that was being spread about it. I have a clipping here that I took from one of the local newspapers. It sets out the fact that while that committee sat and examined the whole question thoroughly, when they brought in their report it was completely the reverse of what was expected.
I Mr. Gillis.]

I am just going to read the heading of the newspaper report I have seen about it. It says this:
A remarkable defence and vindication of the British national health service, introduced by the Labour government, has been published by an independent official committee of inquiry. The committee describes the record of the service as "one of real achievement", denies charges of extravagance, approves the general set-up of the service, and recommends that charges to patients should be lowered rather than raised.
Then the story goes on to stress the fact that all the propaganda we have heard in the past has been just so much propaganda and that this independent committee, which reported directly to the government, completely reversed everything that was said over here about that national health program in Britain.
I hope that in the future, whether it be in Ontario, in Quebec or in Nova Scotia, when pronouncements are made on this question of a national health program, they do not still continue to drag that old red herring over the trail, of the failure of the national health program in Britain. It is anything but that. That committee report, according to this press report, completely waves aside all that propaganda.
I mention that because I think it is still a controversial issue. It has to be taken care of in this country. I believe the federal government is convinced today that the provinces, when they make their set-ups, are prepared to go ahead with a national health program. I am sure most of the members of the house realize that this is one of the most important issues in this country today. It is a way in which our people can be helped to the greatest extent. I think it would offset any tax reductions.
Another matter that I think we should stress very strongly is one that was also introduced by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar; that is trying to have the social security legislation in Canada and the rest of the commonwealth countries made reciprocal, if it is possible to do so. There are many people living in this country who come from different parts of the commonwealth. They receive the old age pension. If they could take that old age pension and go back and live in Australia or New Zealand or Great Britain or Ireland that pension of $40 a month, in their places of origin to which they would like to return, would mean three times the purchasing power that it means to them here in this country. Whilst it is something that would have to be worked out and thought about carefully, the time has come when much of our legislation in the social

security field should embrace all the commonwealth countries. I agree absolutely with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar on this particular point.
There are many little things the minister could have done to bring relief to the lower income groups. I want to mention this fact. Take the pay envelope of the average industrial worker-I do not care whether he is in the automobile, steel, or coal industry or what he is in-and look at his weekly deductions, including income tax. You will find how these weekly deductions shown on the envelope of a worker, which reduce his take-home pay considerably, are in effect a tax that is already there for certain purposes. They are charged against his wages. I have looked at some of them and worked out a kind of average. I would say that today the average industrial worker of this country is paying at least $5.35 a week in ordinary deductions for hospital plans, pension plans and that kind of thing. In addition to that, the average income tax that is paid would be approximately $10 a week.
Worked out on a yearly basis, that amounts to a tax of $735.60 a year. The average worker has his income reduced to that extent by items that are already shown on his envelope and that are just as much a tax as his income tax. He has to carry them by virtue of his employment. You may say that it is a form of insurance and that he is going to receive benefit from it at some time. Nevertheless it is a condition of employment that these obligations must be met before his take-home pay is computed. This is a group of people who argue all the time and send us resolutions to the effect that the basic exemptions should be stepped up, that a single person should get an exemption of $2,000 a year and that a married person should have his exemption raised to $3,000 a year. In view of the fact that they are already paying a tax of some $735 a year I think they are on sound ground in asking that the exemptions be raised to the levels I have already mentioned, so as to relieve them of some of the burden they are already carrying as the result of indirect taxes.
There is another item at which I think the minister should have taken a look, the matter of household appliances. When the average young couple get married today they have to buy a refrigerator, a toaster, a little electric range and so on. I believe the excise tax on such items should have been eliminated. It is quite a burden for the average young couple starting housekeeping today when you consider the cost of building a home, if you build one, and then the cost of equipping it.
The Budget-Mr. Gillis

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SUPPLY OF GARRY 27

speechtext:
I think something should have been done in that regard. I was in a home last night where a young couple are struggling to get along, and I have seen the same thing a good many times. They are both working and are trying to get a home together. They have mortgage payments to meet and they want to equip their kitchen. Take a look at what the sales tax means on the items that are required for such a kitchen.
Of course it is too late now to do anything. The budget has been prepared and presented. It is before the house. It is government policy. It is going to go through because the voters of Canada have seen to it that the government has a sufficient number of members in the house to put it through. The only effect our arguments can have is with regard to the super-budget the minister is going to bring in next time. We can provoke his thoughts with regard to cases where he should give some relief if he wants to get votes.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SUPPLY OF GARRY 27
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: An election every year would help.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SUPPLY OF GARRY 27
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I suggest that the minister take a square look at the question of the sales tax on household appliances when he is bringing in his next budget. There is another item about which the minister and I have had a lot of correspondence. I refer to the soft drink industry. There are several small operators in my part of the country who are just struggling along on a shoestring. The difference between the taxes they are carrying and bankruptcy is just as little as that. They have been hanging on hoping the minister would remove the tax, but it has not happened.
If the minister wants to make himself popular and get a lot of miners' votes there are other taxes he could remove. We have also talked about this matter a good many times. The coal miner has to buy certain equipment that goes with his trade. He has to buy a special hat. The Minister of Fisheries will understand this because he is an old miner. The miner has to buy special shoes with steel toecaps. If he is working at the coal face he has to buy his explosives and caps, and these things run into quite a bit of money each year. The request has been made to me time and time again, and this is not the first time I have spoken about the matter in the house, that in view of the fact

The Budget-Mr. Gillis that these things are part of the miner's cost of operation he should be allowed to write them off for income tax purposes. It has not happened to date though I have made the request a good many times, but it may not be a bad idea to get it in the next budget.
There is another matter I have discussed with the revenue department recently. Union dues are deductible for tax purposes. It is clearly stated in the Income Tax Act that annual union dues are deductible, but before you can become a member of most of the unions throughout the country today you have to pay an initiation fee. In some cases it is $50, in others $150, or it may be as high as $200, depending on the union. I have had many people ask me why it is not possible to charge initiation fees as a tax offset in view of the fact that annual union dues are deductible. In discussing the matter with the department that collects taxes it has been pointed out to me that the joker in the act is that annual union dues are specified. The Minister of Finance might get in touch with the Minister of National Revenue and suggest that a change should be made to allow initiation fees as a tax offset, because if it is legitimate to allow annual union dues as an offset I think it follows that it is equally right to allow initiation fees. The deduction of the initiation fee would only take place once in a lifetime, at the time the person joined the union.
Such a move would be a vote catcher. There are many young people joining unions today and having to pay $100 as an initiation fee. At the present time the money is a dead loss to them, and they consider that they should be allowed to offset it.
There is another plea I should like to make to the minister, and it concerns our blind people. I know the budget does not deal specifically with problems of this kind, but indirectly it affects government policy as to whether the relief for which we ask in different cases can be given. The blind people of this country have been sending literature to us from time to time, and I think the government should consider removing the means test from the blind pension at an early date. In the last representation I had from the blind they have this to say about the handicaps of the blind:
In addition, a blindness allowance free from the means test would provide a basic security, and so would be a source of encouragement and lead the blind to greater productivity and higher income. As it is, the means test holds back the allowance recipient from his full earning capacity lest his income forfeit his allowance and yet not be sufficient to provide a livelihood in its own right. Moreover, the means test only adds to the frustration and fear confronting the newly blind, who meet their handicap in adult life. It undermines


ambition and retards the rehabilitation process. A blindness allowance free from the restricting means test can be a positive restoration of selfconfidence.
No income tax is levied against a single sighted man whose earnings are less than $1,000 a year, or against a married man under $2,000. Yet, because of the means test, the single sightless worker may not have more than $840 or the married man more than $1,320.
I think their argument is absolutely sound. If these people, with the handicap they have and receiving the blind pension of $40 a month, have the courage to go out and tackle the world, sell brooms, sell pencils or run canteens and thus earn something on the side for themselves, I do not think they should be penalized by the loss of what I consider a disability pension rather than a means of livelihood.
During the course of this and other debates in the house I have listened to members comment from time to time on the group with which I sit and the movement I represent. They have used some pretty loose language in the interpretation of the policy and program of the C.C.F. party. But I have noticed that the only authority they had for the interpretation they made was that free enterprise was a wonderful thing; that it had saved the world, the sun and the moon, and that anyone who came into the picture with a little different opinion did not have any right to exist. They pick up a copy of the Globe and Mail or a copy of the Montreal Gazette or of some other newspaper, read an editorial from it and say, "That is what they stand for".
I sat here and heard it from the other side of the house, and from this side, during this session. I therefore thought it would not be a bad idea if during the course of this session some time somebody dug up an authoritative statement by someone who is in the C.C.F. movement and who has some responsibility. If I want to get an opinion on a point of law I go and see a lawyer about it; or if I am sick I go and see a doctor. At least he is qualified to make a diagnosis of the particular problem on which I may he questioning him. I certainly will not go to an ultra free-enterpriser in order to get an interpretation of what the C.C.F. program may be.
I thought I knew the C.C.F. policy and program fairly well, but during the course of the debates to which I listened I began to wonder whether over the last nine or ten years they had changed to the extent that these arguments would lead you to believe. I therefore went back into my archives and I looked up some authorities. In getting us an interpretation of what the C.C.F. program and policy really mean, I figured that the best authority I could find in Canada would be someone who has been with the movement,

who has responsibility in the movement and who has some responsibility to the public.
The best man I could find was the present premier of Saskatchewan, Tommy Douglas. When he made this statement he had been premier of Saskatchewan for some five years. He is premier of a province in which he was elected on the C.C.F. ticket. He has been administering a C.C.F. program for five years, and he is giving to the people who elected him an account of his stewardship on this particular point of what the C.C.F. means. I think he should know as much about it as the editor of the Globe and Mail, the editor of the Ottawa Journal or anyone else, because to my mind he exemplifies what I thought the
C.C.F. was and he is doing that kind of job.
I have heard thrown at us the statement that the C.C.F. will socialize your second pair of shoes, that the government are socialists in silk hats because they support the C.B.C., which is a monopoly, and the T.C.A., which is a monopoly. Someone over here said he would rather have a private monopoly than a government monopoly. I do not think there is much difference. There is only one corner of our community in this country where I can see any monopoly, and that is in this corner of so-called competitive free enterprise which does not exist. There is no such animal in this world any longer. If there were, there would not be the need for groups such as mine and such as we have to the left of us here.

We hear of this business of free enterprise. It is not free any longer, and it is not enterprise. The man who is trying to get a living in this world from a small business has a hard row to hoe. I therefore asked myself the question, have we slipped to the point where we are going to do all the things that we are accused of, or have the program and policy got into such a mess today that nobody knows where he stands?
Hence I went back and thought I would get an interpretation from Tommy Douglas. Many of us in this house know him. We have complete faith in his honesty and integrity. The people of Saskatchewan certainly think a great deal of him. He said this in 1949, and that program has not changed one iota. I should just like to put it on the record for the purpose of keeping the record straight, as I did with this inquiry by the British government into the validity of the national health program in that country. It is official. When you talk about socialism in the loose and illiterate way that a great many people talk about it, and when you consider the many types of socialism there are and have been in the 67509-174
The Budget-Mr. Gillis world, I think it is nearly time that we in this group put back on the record exactly what we mean when we say we would do certain things to protect the public with regard to much of the monopoly control that exists today, not through the government but outside of it.
I will take extracts from this talk on the subject of where we stand with regard to the organization of the economy of this country. I am going to quote Tommy Douglas on that subject, and I might say that I do so with approval. I agree 100 per cent with what he says here. It has always been my conception of this movement. He says:
There are three different types of ownership in which we believe-
That has been the discussion, ownership.
-private ownership, co-operative ownership and public ownership, and each of these may again be subdivided, as I will explain later.
Let us take private ownership first, for under a C.C.F. government private ownership will always compose the greater part of our economy. It was largely because of the loss of private ownership of our farms and our homes and small businesses through the growth of monopoly and the control of credit that the C.C.F. was first organized- organized to get ownership back, not to destroy it. Private ownership can be divided roughly into two classes, individual ownership, and partnership or company ownership. In this field would come your home, your farm, retail businesses, secondary industries, services industries, except transportation and communications, and a host of others. As a matter of fact we believe that with increased production and better distribution made possible by a balanced economy we would have more, not less, private ownership. You have only to look around you at the stores in any town of over 1,000 population and see the numbers of them that are chain-operated or controlled to see what is happening in our economy today. The small businessman in retail, processing and manufacturing is being ruthlessly pushed aside, and this is becoming more apparent as supply catches up with demand and business becomes more competitive.
That was written in 1949. You can see that he was not far out, when you consider that last year in this province alone, according to reports, there were some 6,000 small business failures. These failures were in your local grocery set-ups, where the Loblaw stores and the A & P stores and such people come in and do the kind of business financing with which the small operator cannot compete. Mr. Douglas goes on further and says this:
Don t let anyone tell you therefore that the C.C.F. does not believe in private ownership. We do. As a matter of fact the greatest enemies of private ownership today are the monopolies who are condemning the C.C.F. They distract your attention by weird tales and misrepresentation of C.C.F. policy while they blackjack you and send you to the receivers.
He is talking to the small businessman. Anyone who knows Tommy Douglas knows that is his language. He continues:
Co-operative ownership is the second type of ownership in which the C.C.F. believes. It operates

The Budget-Mr. Gillis
in both the producer and consumer fields. In both of these fields it creates the necessary competitive factors to assure efficient and reasonable service. It retains in the community the largest possible amount of the wealth created by the community. It creates and stimulates the ability for selfhelp and self-reliance in solving the economic problems facing the individual in a free society. It is a training ground for leadership in the community and is a most effective weapon in fighting the growth of monopoly control. The growth of the co-operative movement in every part of the world has coincided with the development of the social democratic movements in the same areas. The one creates the economic freedom and intelligent group self-interest which is essential to the growth of the other. Co-operative ownership means a wider and more democratic distribution of ownership which is the objective of democratic socialism.
Finally, the C.C.F. believe in public ownership. This is again divided into three fields-municipal, provincial and federal, each having its own place. It is not now, and never has been, the intention of the C.C.F. to centralize all public ownership under the federal government. It would be equally as foolish for the federal government to take over ownership of the transportation systems of Toronto or Regina as it would be for those cities to own and operate the Canadian National or Canadian Pacific Railway within their boundaries. Public ownership has been proven a success in many fields and is being expanded today by even the capitalist government of the U.S.A. Even they recognize that complete private ownership in certain fields carries with it powers which they dare not leave in private hands. The Catholic Archbishop of Australia in 1949 issued a statement condemning total socialization, but stating, and I quote "the church recognizes that, under present conditions, there are certain forms of enterprise and industry which are of quite extraordinary importance to the community and which may legitimately come under public control. Among these are banking and insurance, the manufacture of steel and heavy chemicals, rail, sea and air transport, public utility services (electricity, gas, tramways) and armaments". This list goes even further than the proposals of the C.C.F. platform.
There are, however, two forms of ownership to which the C.C.F. is unalterably opposed. The first is complete state ownership as advocated and practised by communism, and the other is monopoly and cartel ownership as developed under capitalism. We agree wholeheartedly with the council of the Christian churches in their statement issued in Amsterdam in 1949, when they stated that "the idealogies of communism and of laissez-faire capitalism are equally wrong".
I could go on, but I know my time is running out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every time I have spoken in the house I have done so to give my views on matters of public interest and, for the past sixteen years I have tried to reflect here the opinions of my electors. If there is one matter which deeply interests them at present, and about which they send me numerous requests for information, it is that of health insurance, of hospital insurance.
Throughout my public life I have been a supporter of social security. Early in life I had to work and assume responsibilities; my family bravely faced situations which would not have existed if, in those days, there had been beneficial social legislation like that which is in force today. I have therefore considered it my duty to champion the cause of the lowly, the hard worker and the needy. The people of Canada do not want humiliating public charity, but rather legislation that would enable underprivileged citizens in this rich and prosperous country to get their share of welfare and security.
I am happy to underline here the vast accomplishments of the Liberal party to which I belong, and which was successfully led by Mr. Mackenzie King until 1948 and which has been led with no less success since by the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent. Even opponents have to recognize that the Liberal party, which has governed the destinies of our country without interruption since 1935, has always enjoyed the confidence of the Canadian people; it has enjoyed that confidence during the worst period of the war and it came out of it with an even greater prestige than before. Today it still enjoys that confidence. The social legislation enacted by our party has been the envy of other countries and has helped to create in Canada an atmos-
The Budget-Mr. Bertrand phere of welfare that has become indispensable.
Nobody would like to see family allowances stopped; the government that enacted that legislation made a generous gesture and the people cannot forget it. If it did not exist, we would have to enact it. That legislation has been greatly beneficial to our people; it has satisfied a human desire for protection and provided help for the family. In the last few years, several requests have been made asking that the allowances be doubled, without increasing taxes. In my opinion, such a request was improperly put forward. I have often said and I still contend that although I am in favour of increasing family allowances, I do not see how it could be done without increasing one way or another governmental expenses and, therefore, the taxes which we have to pay.
I believe, and I have often said so in my constituency and in the house, that the family allowances act should be revised. It was enacted nearly eleven years ago. By virtue of that legislation, the government has spent several million dollars, but that money has not been wasted. It has contributed to the health and the progress of the nation. Those dollars have provided better food, better care, better clothes and a better education for thousands of children. The family allowances cheque, which comes at the same time, on the same day of each month, which is paid without political partisanship and used to good purpose has contributed and still contributes to create an atmosphere of family satisfaction which honours our country. During the past eleven years, the cost of living has greatly increased. I believe that the time may have come to revise the act, to set new rates that would take into account the cost of living. The Department of National Health and Welfare would be well advised to study the matter. In adjusting the act to present conditions, it would answer the general wishes of the people.
By providing good food and a good education to our young citizens we are doing an act of liberation. Children truly represent the future. If our children are healthy, our future will be prosperous; if our children are well educated and understand their religious, civil and patriotic duties, our future will be assured. Money invested by Canada to educate our citizens of tomorrow is not lost. It is an asset which enhances the undeniable prestige of our country.

The Budget-Mr. Bertrand
Mr. Speaker, I put on the order paper of the house a motion which has not been debated but which deals more particularly with the blind. I have always taken an interest in them, and I know the work done by their associations, especially the Societe amicale des aveugles, in which I am particularly interested. In my opinion, the blind should not be subjected to a means test; they should be granted the maximum pension without any restriction whatsoever. True, last year the age requirements were lowered and the maximum income permitted was increased, but that does not seem to be sufficient. Few blind people in Canada have an income sufficient to provide for themselves, and the majority are unable to cope with the monthly allowance they receive unless they do some other work to supplement their income. I recently said in a speech in this house;
The blind are not deprived of all their producing capacities, but these capacities are deadened or reduced to nothing. If you want the blind to take on some productive job, you have to make them financially secure. The psychological fear of not being able to keep up their jobs because they might lose their pension if they kept on working adds to their anguish.
I have not changed my mind. In the case of the blind, one must stimulate and not destroy their human ideal. The elimination of the means test would guarantee their financial security as, by the very nature of things, blindness entails expenses which people with normal vision are spared: higher cost of living, guide services, additional maintenance costs, more adequate medical care, poor health, etc. Blindness calls for many extra expenses. It is for that reason that quite a substantial number of blind people in the province of Quebec do not get the pension. The husband or wife is working, since the maximum income fixed by law, even with a full pension, is not always adequate for the maintenance of the home. Therefore, in many cases, the blind person lives outside the home in order to receive full pension, leaving to the spouse the responsibility of working and raising the family. To raise the family and social standard as well as the dignity of the blind, it is essential that the blind do not have to suffer an inferiority complex throughout the year. The blind person lives in darkness; in many ways, his existence is complicated; he worries and loses patience, he feels lonesome and forsaken. The elimination of the means test would open new perspectives to him; he would find a new reason to work, to adapt


himself to circumstances and thus, being less worried, be in a better position to provide for the education of his children and the maintenance of his family.
I wish to say a word about disability allowances; no one should blame me for a few remarks on this subject since I have advocated this pension many years before the legislation on this matter was put on our statute books.
The provinces have accepted the act, although reluctantly in some cases. The regulations have been approved following discussions between representatives of the federal government and of the provinces. Some 30,000 people now get the disability pension in Canada, which is much less than the 50,000 and more which had been estimated at one time. Personally I think that the act is too rigid, and a great many cases which have been called to my attention after the applications had been rejected have brought home to me that it is so. Many of these applications have been submitted anew, and they have been granted favourable consideration.
I do not think this legislation should be for the dying; it should become more flexible. We could consider as invalids a large number of people who, though they may not be forced to remain constantly in bed or in a chair are prevented, through some infirmity or other, from earning their living or are constantly refused on the labour market, even though they may have the use of their hands or feet. A number of applications which seemed worthy of consideration have apparently been refused. The lack of latitude provided for in the regulations would seem to be directly responsible for this. Would it not be well to call for a study of these applications which have been turned down in order to see whether or not the present regulations could be changed so as to make the legislation really efficient and to achieve the desired purpose?
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say to the government that the constituency of Terrebonne, which I represent in this house, supports a national health insurance plan and that my constituents are anxious for it to be quickly implemented. The comments which I have heard and the views which I have had the opportunity of ascertaining are quite indicative of the opinion of the people on this subject. If my constituents entertain such definite views on this matter, I doubt whether things are at all different in other constituen-

cies. It must be recognized that, for our working people, insecurity is the worst worry of all. There is nothing like idleness to wipe out in a few weeks savings which have been acquired after long and arduous effort, and to turn a prosperous home into one beset with financial difficulties or even with real want. These views of my constituents are all the more welcome to me because ever since I have been in public life I have never ceased to demand legislation which would ensure our working people the help of the nation in case of illness or confinement to a hospital.
I do feel also that most people in Canada favour a national health insurance plan and that the decision of the government to go ahead in this matter has been highly appreciated. I would even go further. The people of this country would not forgive the government if it were to stop halfway now, no more than it would forgive delay in completing the present program of social security by this beneficent legislation. And I would add that this question is so close to the heart of the people and appears so essential to them now that provincial governments refusing to co-operate may be judged severely by their constituents.
It is becoming impossible for the low income group to face the excessive costs of hospitalization. I realize that a hospital, like a hotel, must ask rates which often appear prohibitive, in order to meet their costs of management, but it is none the less undeniable that medical and hospital costs are excessively high. Dr. Jean Gregoire, deputy minister of health in the province of Quebec, did not hesitate to say a few months ago that 80 per cent of the people of Quebec-and I presume that such is the case elsewhere-cannot meet hospitalization expenses when they are sick. No doubt, there are many Canadians who are protected at this time against medical and hospital costs, either by subscribing to a private hospitalization plan or because their employers have adopted a group insurance plan which protects them, together with their dependents. There remains, however, a great number of Canadians-possibly more than 50 per cent of them-especially in the working and low income classes, who have no protection at all. It may be because their trade does not permit it, or because their employers are opposed to it or never thought of it, or because their salary does not allow them to join a private insurance plan. If their income is not sufficient to
The Budget-Mr. Bertrand permit them to seek preventive medicine, all the more reason for their being unable to face hospitalization costs. These people, I should point out, even when sick, will wait to the last minute before seeing the doctor, because of the very inadequacy of their income. They will conceal their ailment and suffer in silence, seeking relief from sedatives and old wives' remedies.
When the time comes for them to be hospitalized, they will not only be unable to regain their health but they will have to bear the handicap of impaired health. That point of view should be kept in mind by those organizations which, in their annual briefs or in their periodical suggestions to governments, will not come out clearly for or against the health insurance scheme but which say that we must be careful and proceed slowly, under the barely concealed pretext that taxes might go up.
On the other hand, many welfare and labour organizations are asking for that social security measure, and if the price comes high -which nobody will deny-they say that if we can, and rightly so, spend huge amounts of money to protect ourselves against outside dangers, against war and even to prevent war, it is up to the government to build a large social security system in order to suppress as much as possible social evils, to do away with distress which comes from ill-health, and to give Canadians, in these times of anxiety, the benefit of security and the priceless advantages of good health. The English writer and statesman Benjamin Disraeli said on that score:
The health of the people is really the foundation upon which all their happiness and all their powers as a state depend.
Our country is not backward in the public health field. Under the constitution, public health comes under provincial jurisdiction; but, eight years ago, the federal government embarked upon a national health program for the sole reason that the provinces alone could scarcely establish a uniform system and that it seemed necessary therefore, without depriving them of their autonomy, to co-operate with them on a national level so as to give greater efficiency to all freely taken joint decisions. Thousands of beds have been put at the hospitals' disposal; from year to year, medical research has gained in importance, public courses have been initiated, groups have been formed with the help of the various governments, and great progress has been

The Budget-Mr. Bertrand made in the fight against tuberculosis, cancer, mental illness and other ills that plague humanity. And-I am stressing this without fear of contradiction-never has the country had a better minister to carry out all these plans in the field of social security, i.e. family allowances, old age pensions, pensions for the blind, and for the disabled, than the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). I am therefore happy to pay a deserved tribute, not only to his personal talent, but also to his devotion for his cherished cause of public health, to his remarkable and well known industry, and to his very clear comprehension of all problems under his departmental jurisdiction.
I am among those who hope that he will be able to carry out the health insurance scheme. This is a vast project indeed, but his devotion measures up to it. I know he understands the importance of this scheme, and that he wants to help all Canadians, and more particularly the small wage earner.
The small wage earner is the man who, in order to live and support his wife and children, has to count on each day's work, who cannot afford to be ill for, whenever he is, hardship immediately befalls his home. The small wage earner is the one who never achieves wealth and who, at the end of his days, after toiling for forty years, has painstakingly put aside only a few hundred dollars to cope with unforeseen expenses of sickness and old age. The small wage earner who, during his lifetime, has been able to escape, with his wife and family, surgical and hospital bills which are always heavy will be, among his kind, a very lucky man indeed. Many of these people come to my office and show me unpaid hospital bills. They are people who, over and above their daily cares, always feel tortured by the same bills which will keep on piling up. Hospitals want to be paid; they cannot carry on unless they are. Are patients always able to pay? That is the question. Health insurance will be beneficial both to our citizens, who have to cope with sickness and to the hospitals whose progress will thus be ensured.
The small wage earner is the one who, week after week, sees his tax deducted from his pay cheque, and, though sometimes grudgingly, is nevertheless willing to do his share in the administration of the country. And when he makes out his annual income tax return, what is he allowed to deduct? A few dollars as charitable donations, a portion, always insignificant, of his medical expenses. On the other hand, the industrialist, the merchant, the businessman, owing precisely to their business, have an expense account where they can enter so many indirect expenses, the legal

facility of providing themselves with leisure and amenities, and to bestow on their families benefits squarely denied the low income class. Thus, health insurance would create a new balance through which the well to do would lose nothing of their benefits, while the poor and the humble would get their share of security. The happiness of the lower class is made of peace of mind and heart. You cannot have one without the other. Let us not forget that the heaviest damage to health is not caused by work, because sixty year old workers, who have worked very hard all their lives, still go to work early every morning. The things that are harmful to health, that undermine and destroy it, are moral and financial worries. Just go down to the miserable classes of society, and you will see what it is all about. The low income worker will understand that, even though he has to contribute his share to the establishment of a health insurance plan, he no longer will have, when misfortune strikes him, the awful shame of having to tell his doctor or the hospital officials that he is unable to pay, of having to be endlessly hurt in his feelings, and of having thereafter, because of accumulated debts, to live in discouragement, and sometimes on the brink of despair. We, the lucky ones, must keep aware of the fact that, close to our home there are slums, and people who, through lack of money, have never paid a visit to their native province or country and who will never go to Florida, and we must convince ourselves, when we criticize a poor home with a television set, that the poor ones too must have their moments of enjoyment. In these times of easy life, when sports are draining so much money, when the attraction for travel increases from year to year, when luxurious restaurants are crowded with customers who do not care for the amount of the bill, when in grills and bars we pay as much as one dollar for a glass of scotch or rye, I will never tolerate that those with an easy life should be the first to criticize or to refuse to pay a few additional dollars in taxes in order to maintain and develop our social security plan.

Before the house adjourned at six o'clock I was speaking of health insur-*

ance. I would like to repeat one sentence I said at that time.
We, who are more favoured, should take note of the fact that next to us there are slums, that there are people who, through lack of money, have never visited their province, or their country, who will never see Florida; before criticizing the poor people who own television sets, we should stop and think that those poor people are also entitled to a few moments of happiness. In this period of easy living, where sports drain so much money, where the thirst of travelling increases from year to year, where luxury dining rooms are overcrowded with customers who do not worry how much the bill will be, where people have to pay as much as one dollar for a glass of scotch or rye in grills or bars, I will never admit that those who are better off are the first to criticize or to refuse to pay a few more dollars in taxes for the maintenance and the development of our social security program.
To maintain a social security program and, if need be, to improve it, is to destroy communism. Has communism ever been associated with a high level of production, attractive salaries and a high standard of living? Does communism make any headway in countries where the government is concerned with the lot of the working class and of people of modest means and takes care of the needy, the sick, the destitute and the poor? Has communism any chance to grow in a country where social legislation protects the people against the hazards of life and ensures the welfare of the needy? No one who is sincere would refuse to pay a few dollars a year in taxes in order that the government may enact a social legislation which is not only helping the population but ensures internal peace to a country like ours.
Personally, I would be willing to pay more taxes if necessary for the implementation of a health insurance program. There is no need to throw everything upside down nor to establish state medicine.
It is not a matter of preventing the family from choosing its own physician. Nor is it a matter of controlling the hospitals or the organizations which are in charge of them. The autonomy of the provinces can and must be respected. The federal government is willing to pay half the costs of such a health insurance plan. True, if it does need the approval of six provinces to go ahead, I hope that it wins it as quickly as possible and that the province of Quebec will be among those six.
However, should this national health insurance plan meet with too many difficulties, should the provinces refuse to enter into it
The Budget-Mr. Montgomery for a number of reasons into which I need not go, I still think that the government should not close this case it has opened in the interest of the whole country. It should put the question to the voters at the next election or, should circumstances become pressing, ask for a referendum so as to settle the matter once and for all.
Mr. Speaker, our social security program makes our people happy. The people know that they owe it to the party to which I belong. This program cannot and must not be tinted by politics. It is not and that is to the credit of all of us representing the people here. If old age pensions did not exist today on a national scale for people of 70, how many people and how many homes would be in difficulty. The amount of $40 a month was a boon to public health. It helps and continues to help old people to get better treatment and, by casting off financial worries, it enables a great many people to live longer and to await in serenity the inevitable twilight. The thing that must prevail now is a feeling of security, the certainty of that security. By spending annually enormous amounts of money for NATO and the protection of its territory, our country gives us that certainty. That feeling of security must also be felt in every home and be solidly anchored in the heart of every Canadian. Health insurance must become one of the foremost concerns of this government and also of parliament. In this as in other fields, I know, the government will not fail and it is our duty, in this parliament, to support the government.
