speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate I should like to speak to two items in particular, but first I should like to make a few comments.
The budget held no surprises for me except the discriminatory tax imposed on a few United States magazines. This has been very ably dealt with by the hon. member for Calgary South, himself a publisher of Canadian trade journals and one who, I believe, can speak with authority. It has also been dealt with by other speakers. So I shall have nothing further to say on that.
As regards agriculture and the farmers, I find nothing substantially new that will help this particular industry. There are some changes in the tariff items which may clarify some former rulings, but in general there is nothing I can see that will give any great uplift to our farmers, or assure them of any relief from the price-cost squeeze, or enable them to obtain a greater share of the consumer's dollar.

The Budget-Mr. Montgomery
Among certain tariff items referred to the tariff board during the past year was that of potatoes. Whilst no definite action has been taken, I was interested in the minister's announcement that he hoped to be able to make a statement in the very near future in connection with that particular item. I trust that this will be a statement of policy that will be satisfactory to the producers. There are a great many growers of potatoes in my constituency, and this is a product that greatly affects the economy of my province, as it is one of the largest cash crops produced in New Brunswick.
The minister also announced that he was not recommending any reduction in the general level of the income tax, but that there would be some minor changes in certain provisions and such contemplated changes would be announced when the amending bill was brought in. Again I trust that among those changes he has in mind will be one restoring to section 42 of the Income Tax Act the true intent, meaning and spirit which I am sure members of this parliament had in mind when those sections were amended a few years ago; that is, the sections applying to farmers and fishermen. It is a well-known fact that the incomes of farmers and fishermen fluctuate greatly from year to year, and the legislation was an attempt, in my opinion, to deal equitably with individuals in these occupations.
This has particular application to farmers in my province, whose chief crop is potatoes. In some years their income is fairly good. In fact in some instances it is quite large, owing to good yields, high prices, selling at the right time and many other factors. However, in other years-and unfortunately we have a good many of the other years-owing to adverse weather conditions, poor yields and low prices, the incomes of the farmers are not good. In fact it is not uncommon for many of them to have losses, and they are lucky if they break even.
This is all due to factors over which the farmer really has no control. This legislation to which I refer was designed to give the farmer and fisherman some remedy in combating such uncontrollable circumstances. Section 42 was intended to permit farmers whose chief source of income was their farming operations to average their income over a period of five years if they elected to do so. In other words the farmer or fisherman was permitted to select any five-year period. He must not use the same years in different periods, but if he has selected a five-year period the interpretation of the section seems to be clear that he is not required to file a return or to pay a tax within that period.

That interpretation was upheld by Mr. W. C. Fisher, Q.C., of the income tax appeal board in the case of Topham v. The Minister of National Revenue. It seems to me there is no way of telling whether the farmer has any income tax to pay until the end of the five-year period. He may have a very good income in one or two of the years, but I think it was the intention of parliament when it passed the legislation to give the farmer and the fisherman the opportunity of waiting until the end of the selected period. Then if he was taxable he would have the right to average his tax over that period and pay it at that time.
However, the Department of National Revenue did not agree with Mr. Fisher. The department appealed the decision. The case went to the exchequer court and the decision was reversed. The reversal, if I understand the situation, was made on the basis of the interpretation placed upon section 44 of the act. You are all familiar with that section of the act. It provides that in so far as an individual is concerned he must file an income tax return for any year in which he is taxable, and he must pay his tax. This must be done within a certain period which is laid down in the section. The minister is also supposed to prescribe the form to be filed and the information which he requires. Under subsection 2 of section 44 the minister may call upon a person to file a return within a certain period, whether or not they are taxable, and if they do not do so they are liable to the penalties provided in section 55.
I am not going to criticize the decision of the exchequer court because I understand just as well as anyone that lawyers and judges differ in their opinions on interpretation, but I want to bring this point to the attention of the minister and the government. Under the ruling of the exchequer court farmers and fishermen have lost the right which I believe parliament intended to give them in order to correct the situation that the legislation was intended to correct. Under this ruling a farmer must file a return in any year in which he thinks he has made enough money to be taxable, and he must pay the tax. If he does not file the return and pay his tax he is subject to the penalties under section 55.
It works out in this way. Suppose the farmer has a good year in the second year of the period he has selected and his income is taxable. Under the present interpretation he must file a return for that year and must pay his tax on the basis of that year alone. But at the end of three more years, which would be the end of his period, is the only time at which it can be determined by either the farmer or the income tax department whether

or not he has any tax to pay, and I claim that when the farmer is forced to file a return and pay tax in the second year he is penalized because he is deprived of certain money for the next three years, if at the end of the period he finds he has no taxable income for the whole period which he has selected. Second, the farmer is subject to the penalties of section 55.
I submit that this situation is working hardship on the farmer, and I bring the matter to the attention of the minister and the government because I believe sincerely that parliament passed the legislation with the intention of providing a remedy for people with fluctuating incomes who may have one good year, two good years and three bad years, so they could average their income over the period and if they had no taxable income for the period they would then have no tax to pay.
I think that was what parliament intended, and I believe that intention has been frustrated by the decision of the court in the same way that other intentions with respect to the act have been frustrated. I believe the minister referred to that in his budget speech. It may be that I am premature in my remarks, but I hope the minister has in mind bringing in an amendment to remedy the situation, because I believe the amendment to section 42 has been affected by the changed interpretation of section 44, which says that every individual who is taxable in a given year must file a form. Inasmuch as the amendment to section 42 provided a five-year period instead of one year, and because there is no definite way of finding out whether or not a man is taxable until the end of the selected five-year period, I contend that section 44 does not apply.
At the present time the farmer is being penalized, and I suppose the fisherman too. I am more interested in the farmers, and I would certainly ask the minister to give the matter thorough study. I should like to see an amendment introduced which will fully restore the original purpose of section 42 and the amendment thereto, in order that farmers will not be severely penalized and to carry out the intention , of parliament. Otherwise I do not see much use in having the amendment.
As a matter of fact, I see nothing in the act which directs the government to return to the farmer any money he has paid during the period if it turns out at the end of the period that he is not taxable. He may have paid a small amount during the period but when his income is averaged the result may be that he has overpaid. I know the department has always been very prompt in making 67509-175
The Budget-Mr. Montgomery adjustments of that nature; nevertheless the man is without his money for one, two, three or maybe four years.
The other particular point in connection with the budget on which I should like to dwell for a few minutes is the question of federal-provincial relations. The minister devoted a good part of his address to this subject. He enumerated in a general way the proposals submitted by the federal government to the provinces. He went on to say that under the circumstances the federal government believed that the proposals were eminently fair, reasonable and realistic. He went to quite some length in explaining to hon. members that no province would receive less than it had received under the tax rental agreements.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, these proposals are certainly not in line with what the provinces have a right to expect or with what they had a right to assume was the intention of the Prime Minister in his letter of January, 1955, when he informed the provinces that the government had no intention of abandoning the objective of the tax rental agreements, which was to make it financially possible for all the provinces, whatever their tax base, to perform their constitutional functions and to provide a reasonable level of provincial services without abnormal burdens of taxation. Unfortunately I think the proposals do not achieve this principle, especially for those provinces with a limited tax base such as that which we have in the maritime provinces. Mr. Speaker, it is through no fault of their own that those provinces have not a wider base of taxation.
One of the provincial services that must or should be maintained on a basis of equality throughout this country is education. It costs just as much to erect buildings and provide equipment and other facilities in the maritime provinces as it costs anywhere else. But what do we find? The average cost of education in Canada runs approximately 2-225 per cent of the total Canadian national income but in my own province it would run something like 4-329 per cent of the total income of the people of the province, or almost double.
It might be interesting to some hon. members if I just mention how narrow our tax base is, or the burden of taxation in relation to education in my province; and I think our system is pretty much the same throughout the maritimes. For education alone the municipalities have to pay something like 40 to 45 per cent. How is it done? We have what we call a poll tax. That poll tax is levied on every male person between the ages of 21 and 60, with very few exceptions, and it may run from $3 to as high as $10. That tax is levied

The Budget-Mr. Montgomery regardless of what property a person has, just because he is a male person.
But that is not all. By the way, that tax is for the administration of justice, the hospitalization of the poor, general administration and the services the municipality gives to its citizens. But in addition to that there is another poll tax for educational purposes by which we must raise one-fifth of our share of the operational expenses of education, up to and including the high schools. That poll tax runs anywhere from $5 to $15 and possibly more in some places. And that is not all. Under the system adopted in our province some 10 years ago we also have certain districts getting together, called regional districts, where they build a special school called a regional school and provide not only the ordinary academic courses in education but also a fairly full course of vocational training and sometimes primary agricultural courses. About 40 per cent of the cost of these buildings has to be borne by the district concerned. One-fifth of the cost of the buildings of that district has to be raised by another poll tax, and that poll tax we find runs anywhere from approximately $5 to $20. It will average possibly $18. So the individual has three poll taxes to pay.
In addition to that, every individual man or woman who owns any personal property- that is a car, livestock or any kind of personal property; anything except money or securities-is assessed on its value and the rate is fixed just as the rate is fixed on real estate, and he or she must pay that tax. If people have a truck or a car or things like that they must pay that tax. In addition, of course, we have to pay our tax on real estate the same as people everywhere else. I am speaking of rural districts and small towns such as I have in my constituency. That situation exists all over New Brunswick and I think quite generally in the maritimes. Our real estate is ' assessed. I have checked up on the matter and in comparison with Ontario, percentagewise on the actual value of our real estate, I think we pay higher taxes than are paid in the province of Ontario. I suppose the same comparison would apply with respect to other provinces.
You have that picture, and you can see what a narrow tax base we have. What have we left to tax? In the province of Ontario- I do not know about some of the other provinces-the municipality does not assess anything but real estate. There is no poll tax to pay. There is no personal property tax to pay. You just pay on your real estate, and the mill rate is no greater than ours down there. In some places it is less. I think this is a picture which is possibly overlooked.


Our tax base or whatever you want to call it is limited and our burden is heavy.
Yet with all this taxation, we have not the educational facilities and privileges that are supplied in some of the other provinces. I have mentioned the municipality but the province has to make up the balance, some 60 per cent of the cost; and it is done by grants to teachers on their salaries, grants to the municipality, grants to the school district that builds these schools, grants for transportation of the children and grants for general administration and the running of the schools. This cost is still going up. What has the province left to tax? When the municipality has been assessing the individual there is not much left to the province on which to levy a heavy tax.
In addition to all this you must remember that these small provinces have a difficult time to meet the new demands that call for increased taxes for many types of health services, increased costs of policing and administration, in addition to their regular costs of roads and bridges and all the old expenditures as well which have increased many times in the last few years. Hence my province of which I am speaking at the moment, like the rest of the maritime provinces, is carrying a heavy burden of taxation and is labouring under the difficulty of what we refer to as a narrow tax base. We are limited in area. We are bound by federal fiscal policies which so often operate to our detriment, owing to our location in the federation.
The fiscal policies of the central government which have been necessary and correct-I have no criticism of them-to build Canada into a nation unfortunately have at times handicapped our growth and our trade, and still do so, and have operated to encourage the development of other parts of Canada and the centralization of industry in which we have not shared. I think this has been one of the reasons for the lag in our general economy.
As I said, I am not criticizing this part of the fiscal policy. I think it is right, because this country as a country must grow. I do not think you will find anybody in the maritime provinces who is jealous of the rest of Canada for growing faster. We want to see the nation grow as well. But I think there is a strong feeling in the maritimes- and I do not hesitate to voice it because I feel that I am backed up in it-that there is a responsibility on the federal government to devise and apply a fiscal policy that will even up the whole national economy.
During the past 80 years these three provinces by the sea have contributed much to the progress of this country. I would refer

in particular to the human resources. Many of the leading men and women of our country, who were born down by the sea, have used their ability, initiative and resources in other parts of this great country to assist in making it the nation it is today. We are proud of the fact that wherever you go in Canada you meet hundreds of former maritimers or their descendants. But as a result of the combination of these circumstances and the national fiscal policy, the maritimes have suffered and now lack many of the industries which they ought to have had and which could have been supported. This area necessarily has a limited taxation base and, while a part of this confederation, has not shared in the growth of the nation. Taking all the circumstances into consideration this area has contributed much more to the growth of this country than the central government has properly recognized.
I say therefore, Mr. Speaker, to the Prime Minister and to this government that the proposals submitted to the maritime provinces, the cradle of confederation, in my opinion and in the opinion of many others are not fair, reasonable or realistic as stated by the Prime Minister. Such statements do not measure up to his promise that regardless of the taxation base the federal government should make it financially possible for any province, which would include the maritimes, to perform its constitutional functions and provide reasonable services without having an abnormal burden of taxation. Unless this government is willing to reconsider these proposals or accept other proposals or formulas such as the one submitted by New Brunswick last October, or the suggested appointment of another royal commission similar to the Duncan and White commissions of 1926 and 1934, then conditions will become more difficult.
It will be recalled that the Duncan commission soon found that the economy of these provinces was lagging far behind, and that this was the result of federal fiscal policy and other circumstances over which these provinces had no control. At that time the commission recommended immediate lump sum increases in the federal subsidies, and those recommendations were carried out. They further recommended that another commission be appointed to restudy and reassess the whole economic situation as between the maritimes and the other provinces. This reassessment was carried out by the White commission, and as a result of its report of 1934 the statutory subsidies were further increased in view of the recognition by the members of that commission that the maritime provinces had not received, nor had they any prospect of receiving, the opportunity of 67509-175J
The Budget-Mr. Mclvor access to the central market areas. The commission felt that this was not sharing to an equitable degree in the natural growth of the country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it has been over 20 years since the White commission reported, and in view of the tremendous economic expansion in which the maritimes, as some of the original partners, are entitled to share, I feel the time is overdue for another reassessment by another royal commission of the maritime economic situation as compared with the rest of Canada. I am sure that any commission going into this whole matter would, under all the circumstances, recommend a considerable further increase in our statutory grants or subsidies. In fact I feel that such an increase could run up to 10 times as much as we are getting.
In closing let me say that I feel the government should certainly be considering some of the arguments that were put forward by the maritime premiers during the last conference concerning annual grants and treating this area as a special area. If the government is not willing to do that it is going to be tough for these people to put themselves on an even footing with the rest of Canada. The rest of Canada can grow and will grow, and the gap between us will get wider. I feel it will be nothing short of a tragedy if the maritimes are not treated as a special area. Although it may sound harsh, I feel it will be a blight on this government if it refuses to face up to the situation which we in the maritimes feel calls for justice and a square deal.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SUPPLY OF GARRY 27
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know that I am qualified as a financial critic. While I studied political economy some time ago, yet when I see a budget I feel the need of knowing more. I agree with whoever said that money comes slowly but it goes quickly. I suppose the Minister of Finance finds the same thing. I would say that this is a poor election budget, but it is a great budget for all of Canada. There are some members in this house who would like to have another budget like this next year. I admit that I would like to see another budget like this next year and hear the Minister of Finance say there would be no election that year-not that I am very frightened of anything the future may hold.
It has been said by many in this house and in many of the newspapers that this budget is just holding the line. There are a good many members in this house who have heard that phrase thrown at them enthusiastically, "Hold the line". That is just what our Minister of Finance is doing. There are those who

The Budget-Mr. Mclvor would attack the line. Let us consider inflation. There is a danger of inflation breaking the line. When we have less goods and more money, there is a danger of inflation and the minister has to watch that. There is a danger of unemployment. I sat in this house last year and listened to the oratorical efforts of the opposition in denouncing the government in the matter of unemployment, yet when the government has done its best this year to help cure unemployment we do not hear very much about it. That is one of the dangers of breaking the line.
I think I know some classes of people fairly well. There are those who would tell us to hold the line. Who are they? The big trade unions of Canada want the government to hold the line. They do not want any more unemployment than exists at the present time. The chambers of commerce and the taxpayers of Canada want the government to hold the line. City councils and industries certainly want the government to hold the line; and the question is, will the government hold the line? We call on the Minister of Finance to hold the line because he stands for three fundamental things in the Liberal party, the things on which our party was built.
When we heard the hon. member for Cape Breton South give us the foundation of the C.C.F. party I thought it went back to the Regina manifesto, but our friend told us just what the C.C.F. is. I think I have the right to say on what the Liberal party is built. The minister has shown us, and so has the Prime Minister. The first principle is unity. From Newfoundland to British Columbia we have unity throughout Canada today. Therefore the line is being held. I could speak for half an hour on that, but I do not think it is necessary.
The second thing is security. If you visited any of our schools today what would you see? You would not see what you saw some years ago. From the way the children were dressed some years ago you could tell the brand of flour that had been used in the home. Go out in the streets and look at the automobiles there. Oftentimes I have been ashamed to go around amongst these big cars in my tin lizzy. I know there are some people who are unemployed. The great Teacher said, "The poor ye have always with you." Take a young man who has prepared himself in his youth, who has slaved and toiled like the hon. member to whom we heard such outstanding tributes paid today, who has developed his gifts. Certainly he need not lack a job in Canada today.

The third principle is freedom. We have freedom in Canada. I admit I am free to worship as I like or not to worship at all. I am free to go where I like; I am free even to resign from this house if I thought it was the right thing to do. We are free from the Atlantic to the Pacific to change our employment, to live as we like, to go to sleep when we like and get up when we like and to eat what we like. Since the budget is based upon these three principles of unity, security and freedom we say to the minister, "Boy, you are holding the line".
The reason I rose to take part in this debate is that I have two things to tell the minister. I have been telling him about these things for the past four years. I have been telling him how he should spend some money. But before I do that I think it is my duty to tell him how he can get some. It is all right to cut taxes, but where are we to get some money? We in the Fort William and Port Arthur district have organized the northwestern development association. We put in as the head of that association the city editor of the Times Journal. They are doing an outstanding job in getting industries to come in, and in opening up mines. One of the most outstanding new mines- perhaps you have not heard of it but if you had watched the stock market you could have made a little-is the Iron Bay mines which develop taconite ore in the Red lake district. Dr. Barclay is the man who is taking care of it. He is the former principal of our technical school in Port Arthur.
I must admit that some time ago I was disappointed in our Great Lakes pulp and paper mill, perhaps because of friendship. What is happening? Our northwestern development association is co-operating. They are building two more mills at a cost of $40 million. Perhaps that might not be the correct figure, because I am not a financier, but it is costing a lot of money and it will employ many people. Therefore I say to the minister, you are going to get a lot more taxes from the people who will be employed in producing what will come from that mill.
The two things I am again going to ask the minister to consider-and it is the fourth time I have mentioned them; they say that constant dripping will wear away a stone- are, first, superannuated pensioners, men who retired before salaries were increased. I have a letter from a postman who served 37 years, until one of his legs played out and the other one was not very much better. He was earning $116 a month and when he retired his pension was $88.46 a month. When Blue Cross and hospitalization are taken from that what is left for a couple to live on, especially when his wife is seriously ill? His

salary was $1,600 a year, compared with $3,400 a year today. I should like to tell the minister just as emphatically as I can that this is one of the outstanding needs in Canada today. The pensions of these superannuated pensioners should be increased.
The second thing-and I have a resolution on the order paper today dealing with it-is that pensions should be provided without a means test to veterans 60 years of age and over who saw active service. I said before that I have known some men who had four Christmas dinners in the trenches. I was talking to one a little while ago. He is only 61 years of age, but I could handle him in any way I wished and I am 20 years older than he is. He lost more than 10 years of his life. Why should those men who sacrificed their lives, their home influences and sometimes their homes, not get their pension without a means test at 60? I think it is time we woke up. I just say to the minister I hope that the new money that comes from my district will be used for that purpose.
Our city of Fort William tried to cooperate with the Department of Labour in another way to cure unemployment. This year they decided on winter work. They decided to lay sewers and put a tunnel under the Kaministikwia river for their water which comes down from Loch Lomond. Instead of putting it through the pipes that were broken not long ago, they put in a tunnel where it will be safe for all time.
We think the work which is being carried on now should have some support from the government. I believe that $310,359 was spent on winter work including trunk sewers. I ask the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Finance-and I suppose the Prime Minister will listen-for 20 per cent of that cost. I think we should get 20 per cent of it because I believe it is better to pay out money for that type of work than to pay it out in the form of unemployment insurance or relief.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to express through you my appreciation for several improvements. I patronize the cafeteria upstairs quite frequently because the meals are well prepared; one can eat as much or as little as one likes, and one only pays for what one eats. The improvement in the cafeteria has been outstanding and in expressing my appreciation for this improvement I am sure I am speaking for a good many hon. members in this house.
I would also like to express appreciation for the improvement in the lighting in this chamber. We do like to see the light coming down from above, and with this improvement it is possible for one to see all the clocks in this chamber. We express appreciation for the
The Budget-Mr. Mclvor improved lighting arrangement. I am reminded of the quotation, "Let there be light".

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SUPPLY OF GARRY 27
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I now wish to speak about a pet subject of mine. I think everyone should be interested in games. I am sure, however, that many of us have been disappointed in the great national game, hockey. I saw one game recently and it reminded me of what I wanted to see when I was a boy. I wanted at that time to go to Donnybrook fair where you could get a drink or two and where the slogan, "If you see a head, hit it" prevailed. That hockey game was somewhat like that. It is no longer a matter of playing the game and observing the rules.
I see great hope for the future, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps you have heard mention on the radio of a sports college in Canada. Among the personnel of that sports college is General H. D. G. Crerar. The college publishes a paper which is called Sports College News. This sport's college is a national non-profit organization which is dedicated to helping to raise the standards of amateur sports, efficiency, physical fitness and recreation in Canada. It has been operating on a national basis since 1946. I would like to read to you the objectives of this sports college, as outlined in the March, 1956, issue:
The fundamental objective of the Canadian amateur sports and physical fitness development service is to make Canadians the most amateur sports and fitness conscious and knowledgeable people in the world. In working to this objective the Canadian amateur sports and physical fitness development service will attempt to accomplish the following:
1.	Create increased interest and participation in physical fitness activities throughout Canada.
2.	Stimulate increased participation in amateur sport.
3.	Develop increased interest in and support for amateur sports and recreation generally.
4.	Provide an authoritative information-education service to Canadians (individually and in organized groups) on all matters pertaining to sports skills, training, conditioning, physical fitness programs, organization and all related subjects.
5.	Offer a national "voice" through which those at work in this field can receive publicity and promotional aid in selling their activities to the public and through which support can be generated.
I appreciate the contribution of this group of men who are devoting their time and energy to building up amateur sports in Canada. I must admit that I would rather see a group of pee wees play, go out and throw themselves into their game, than all the professionals in Canada. I think this sports college is to be congratulated, and I hope it will carry on and continue to do its best.
I congratulate the minister on his budget. He did not reduce taxes but he did not increase them very much. Therefore he is

The Budget-Mr. Hahn holding the line, and I expect he will hold the line in such a way that he will be able to hold up his head and look the whole world in the face.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your patience.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SUPPLY OF GARRY 27
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the comments which have been made concerning the budget were not totally unexpected. We have heard it referred to as the nothing-nothing and the zero-zero budget. Some people have referred to it as the six-bit budget. I found very little in it to talk about; therefore I do not intend to waste the minister's time in talking about it at any length.
Certain statements have been made, however, to which I would like to refer. An announcement was made with respect to an increase in wages for federal civil servants, which I am satisfied will be met with good wishes and applause from every part of this house. The announcement today that the temporary employees would receive increases along similar lines is also appreciated. My only hope is that those who are in the lower income brackets will soon be the recipients of a sizeable increase in salary. Certainly those who are in the top bracket are not quite so much in need of an increase.

In making his statement today in reply to a question the Prime Minister indicated that part of the discussion in the United States with the president of that country had to do with the imbalance of trade, and with the fact that Canadians felt it was rather undesirable to have too much United States investment in this country. We in this group have long associated ourselves with that theory and that thought. We feel that if possible Canada should be for Canadians. I am pleased, however, that the Prime Minister is realistic enough to realize, as is the Minister of Finance, that if we are going to have an imbalance of trade we had better correct it in some way and allow United States dollars to come in to assist us in expanding our economy.

speechtext:
There were two other problems I had in mind, but I see I will not have time to deal with both of them. I shall devote the major portion of the remainder of my time to the question of social legislation. From time to time I have heard utterances from the government side that there will never be a depression. We have old age pensions, we have old age security, we have war veterans allowances, we have pensions for the blind and for the disabled, we have family allowances and we have unemployment insurance. Undoubtedly all these measures are very valuable in themselves and should take us through a temporary period of decline or depression.
However, there is some difference with respect to this group of pension and insurance measures. There are one or two that are specifically insurance funds, and there are others which are completely dependent upon the ability of the taxpayer to keep the coffers of the Minister of Finance well supplied in order that he can continue to pay. That is completely true under the present orthodox system of finance.
I did note two years ago, however, that we were in a bad way so far as unemployment was concerned. We had the heaviest unemployment in the history of the nation since what are referred to as the dirty thirties. It was apparent to those who studied the situation at all that if such unemployment had continued the fund would have been depleted. However, such was not the case. Certain factors, to which the hon. member for Fort William did not refer, helped. More particularly, the rise of the prosperous economy in the United States helped to take us out of the throes of that very difficult period.
If unemployment had continued at that time there is very little doubt in my mind that the Minister of Finance would have found fewer, and fewer tax dollars in his coffers, with the result that he would have had more and more difficulty in paying for these services, for after all the dollars that our farmers and

labourers pay through income tax are just a reflection of the prosperity of the businessmen of this country.
I was very interested in the reference to small merchants made today by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. It is not an unusual thing for merchants to go bankrupt in this country at the present time. I believe I brought this particular question to the attention of the house a year or so ago. In my one small community alone we find that because of the no down payment cry, four television and electrical stores have gone out of business in the past few weeks. They just cannot compete under a system that permits the sale of goods with no down payment.
The government must make a note of these things if they expect those people to be contented and happy who have had to close their doors because they could not compete with the large merchants referred to a few minutes ago. Competition in itself is one of the finest things this country can possibly have, but not uncontrolled competition making use of the loss leader practice whereby you sell a teakettle costing you $9.25 for $8.95 and make up the difference by issuing credit through loan companies. That is where the bigger stores get their profit, and there must be some measure of control.
I could continue discussing this matter for some time, but if I did so I would lose the opportunity to tell the house how I and thousands of people in this country feel about the assistance that our senior citizens and others should be receiving. The hon. member for Fort William, to whom we listened with some interest, said it was time we woke up. He referred to people on annuities. Yes, it is time we woke up. It is time we woke up to the realization that the dollar of today is not the dollar of yesterday but is only worth 50 cents.
I know that in many respects these are just repetitious remarks so far as the Minister of Finance is concerned. He has heard some of these utterances before. But, Mr. Speaker, it appears that we must continue to draw this matter to the attention of the minister and the government. It is my opinion that in an expanding economy such as that which we now have, continued expansion depends, and should not, wholly upon social welfare. It should depend upon ability of the businessman to get money with which to progress and further expand his business.
Earlier in the session I among others drew to the attention of the government the decline in the return to the agriculturist in comparison with what he had a right to expect a few years ago. I believe the figure that
The Budget-Mr. Hahn was used was something like 6-7 per cent of the gross national income as the proportion received today by the farmer, as compared with the 20 per cent of the population which he represents; and that I think was compared with what we had back in the 1930's.
Mr. Speaker, the agriculturist is not the only man who suffers a decline. We have these people who are on fixed incomes suffering in exactly the same way. The old age pensioner no longer is asking for a hand-out. He does not have to. The old age pensioner of today in all likelihood contributed something to the compulsory contributory fund through income tax up to a maximum of $60 annually. So it is his by right.
This is not a pay as you go policy, it is admitted. Figures prove that the fund is not self-sustaining. However, it is necessary that these people get more money; that is, if they hope to continue living. We have too many instances-certainly they are not all accidents in the city of Vancouver-of people turning on the gas jet, failing to turn it off and being found dead the next day. These happenings, Mr. Speaker, are not just accidents. In many instances they are quite deliberate. I would say it is our responsibility to see to it that they shall not continue.
We have the problem increasing daily. Young men are forced into compulsory retirement. Who wants a man over 45 years of age, we are told. If he has not a trade or a profession he is just shoved from pillar to post. We have not any place for him in our society. We do not take him and train him as we might or as we should. Maybe he is incapable of being trained. But, Mr. Speaker, because he cannot be trained does not necessarily mean that he should be deprived of the right to earn money, or the right to sustenance. The cost of living is out of all proportion today to what the old age pensioner is receiving. I have here the dominion bureau of statistics Daily Bulletin of Tuesday, January 10, 1956, in which the lead item is as follows:
A survey conducted by the dominion bureau of statistics in five metropolitan areas across Canada indicates that families with two to six members in the nation's larger cities spent an average of $6.94 per person on food every week.
That is just under $7 a week, Mr. Speaker. There are four weeks in the month or approximately 30 days. Worked out on a daily basis, it amounts to about $1 a day. In other words, $30 is the average expenditure each person makes in Canada on food. It is little enough that we expect our senior citizens to live on, a mere pittance of $40 a month, especially now that we are paying into a compulsory contributory fund to make it possible for the government to collect a good portion of it back. After all, it costs only

The Budget-Mr. Hahn $50 million; I believe that is the figure we went into the red last year. That in itself should be little enough contribution from the people of Canada to keep these people alive.
I am satisfied that there are others who recognize the problem. They are closer to it than are we. We practically live in this house for six to eight months of the year. We do not see the poorer people in the cities unless we go home. When we contact them directly or indirectly we receive letters from them asking if we cannot do something to give them some help, somehow or in some way. Certainly, Mr. Speaker, the municipalities that have sent letters to me and the newspaper articles that we read from time to time would indicate that there are thousands of people who are aware of the niggardly way in which we treat our senior citizens.
I have one here. It is a year old; in fact it is two years old now. It is from the Vancouver Province of February 18, 1954, but it is just as true today as it was then. I shall refer to another one later. It is headed "Victoria Sets an Example to Ottawa" and reads in part as follows:
The British Columbia government, in promising assistance to old age pensioners who need it, is giving the government at Ottawa a much needed lesson in generosity and justice.
This is that bunch of crackpot Social Crediters in British Columbia. "Justice" is the word the editorial uses, and possibly it is well chosen. In this article they go on to speak of starvation. Later on they tell about the way they would propose to help these destitute people. Not all old age pensioners are destitute. Not all of them require additional help. However, there is a group that requires help or further assistance. Later on the article goes on to say something about recognition by the government here, by the government's own department, of how much it costs individuals to live. It states as follows:
After all, the Minister of Finance at Ottawa collects no tax on the income of a single person over 65 up to $1,500 a year, and none on a married person up to $2,500. The exemption admits that the single person with $1,500 or less cannot afford a tax and that the married person with $2,500 or less is in the same position.
Why, then, treat the pensioner differently? If the ordinary single citizen over 65 needs $1,500 a year, why pretend that a pensioner can get along on less than half that amount?
Mr. Speaker, I would not be one who would ask for $1,500 a year for these old age pensioners. However, I maintain that when in 1954 the government of British Columbia gave $5 more to the pensioners of that province, they required it; and the province recognized that need as does every self-respecting governing body within this nation. The municipalities are much closer to the
(Mr. Hahn.]
situation than we are, as are the newspaper men. They go to these houses where we find these poor, maimed bodies, and they see for themselves what has taken place. Then in 1956 we had a repetition of the same thing in British Columbia. The Winnipeg Free Press Prairie Farmer of February 8, 1956 had this to say under the heading "B.C. pensions to hit high":
Pensioners living in British Columbia will become the highest paid in Canada if budget proposals of Premier Bennett are implemented.
Incidentally I may say that they were implemented. The article continues:
The premier announced February 1 a $5 increase in the $15 bonus paid by the province above the $40 federal pension.
Only four provinces and the Yukon pay supplements to the $40 federal and provincial old age assistance, all of them conditionally, and mainly for shelter requirements.
British Columbia now will pay $20. Saskatchewan pays up to $20-
Perhaps I could be corrected in this, but I believe the Saskatchewan system works in this way. They will pay up to $20 on condition that there is only one individual in a particular household who is in receipt of the old age pension. Otherwise it would be $20 for two people.
-Alberta $15, Ontario $10 and the Yukon $10.
I believe the Yukon payment comes from the federal treasury. There is a recognition in itself of the fact-and it is certainly true, as hon. members will realize-that in the northern part of this country the cost of living is far higher than anything we find in the more densely populated areas.
There are many other articles to which I could refer, Mr. Speaker. Here is one that strikes me as quaint in its own way, when I contrast it with the statement of the dominion bureau of statistics in respect to the cost of living. I have a clipping from the Vancouver Province of Saturday, January 7, 1956, in which the heading is, in bold type, "You can feed 10 on $40 a week". This amounts to $4 per person per week. The dominion bureau of statistics found that it required $6 and some odd cents, on an average, to feed one person for a week. In the face of that finding this kind of trash has no value in so far as presenting the problem in its proper aspect is concerned. You could feed people on less than that. I have seen people go hungry for a day, but that does not mean that month after month from the time you are 60 or 65 years of age you should be expected to live on such a diet.
I do not know that the article gives the complete diet, but it gives the cost of some of the items, and I shall just use one or two to illustrate how misleading an article such

as this can be. It says eggs, $2.16, but it does not say how many or what price per dozen. It says milk, 40 quarts including dried skim, $6.80. I think it must be mostly dried skim, because I do not know anywhere you can buy milk for 16 and 17 cents a quart. The article refers to sugar, 10 pounds for 50 cents. I am not sure how many hon. members are familiar with the price of food, but I question that statement also. It is indicative of the same sleepy-eyed thinking that goes on across this nation. In the meantime, we do have starvation in the midst of plenty.
I have other newspaper clippings here. This one says, "Senior citizens line up for west van housing". It is dated January 12, 1956. These senior citizens require housing and there just is not any for them. This sort of thing is not localized in the city of Vancouver or New Westminster; we find references to it in the newspapers across this nation. Here we have a clipping on which the heading reads, "Oldster issue urgent". It is taken from the Ottawa Citizen of May 21. Of course this refers to a statement by Mayor Charlotte Whitton when speaking in New York, and possibly for that reason it may not be given the consideration here it should receive. Then there is another clipping from the Vancouver Province of September 14 which says, "Watch food, Father William". It goes on to explain how these senior citizens require dentures. I do not know how they provide them out of $40 per month. We have another clipping on which the heading is, "Housing other major family welfare poser". Still another says, "Montreal's old people need special housing". Here is a letter headed, "Help for old age pensioners". Another clipping has the heading, "Pensioners need homes and hospitals". I do not suppose any person ever thought they had to go to hospitals. Another clipping says, "Our aged accorded 'miserable' treatment".
These clippings are not taken from Hush publication or Tabloid or any of these other publications that are generally referred to as so much trash. They are taken from the leading newspapers in this nation, and I am satisfied we should pay attention to them. Another clipping says, "Pensioners in dyke shacktown fear eviction". These people fear eviction from old shacks in which we would not keep our pigs in the prairie provinces. There is no reason in the world for that, Mr. Speaker. These people fear eviction because there are no homes for them; they have no place to go. Here is another which says, "Let pensioners live where they please".
This raises another very important question. These people who are today the old age pensioners of this country have contributed to
9,	1956	2765
The Budget-Mr. F. G. Power that pension on a compulsory basis of up to $60 per year, depending on their tax rate. This plan is supposed to assist in meeting this particular problem. These people pay into that fund, yet we deprive the old age pensioner of the right to live where he wishes. Certainly once people reach that age we should take into consideration the fact that they will only be with us for a few years. Their sons and daughters are probably most important in their lives, and they want to spend their few remaining years with them. Perhaps it is a case of having to go to a particular area for health reasons. Possibly they are rheumatic or have arthritis or some other unfortunate sickness which causes them to want to live elsewhere. We deny them that right even after they have paid into this fund.

My election was also, in large measure, a tribute on the part of the electorate to the innumerable and important services rendered to them over the years by my father and predecessor, Senator the Hon. C. G. Power, in whose eminent footsteps I hope to prove a worthy follower. The tradition which he has left me is one of unstinting and devoted service in the interests of the electors of Quebec South, of the city and province of Quebec and of Canada. It is also a tradition of party loyalty and service tempered with clearness and independence of thought. Indeed, it is a tradition which he continues to maintain in his new legislative function, and which I will also endeavour, to the best of my ability, to continue in and out of this house.
And now, Mr. Speaker, I crave your kind indulgence while I say a few brief words about the constituency which I have the honour of representing here and while I discuss certain problems of local interest.
The constituency of Quebec South comprises generally speaking that part of the city of Quebec where the Palais station, the harbour, the Battlefields park, the walled town and upper town are located. It also includes the. city of Sillery which is undergoing a rapid growth. Within its limits is to be

The Budget-Mr. F. G. Power found the first permanent European settlement in Canada. It has felt the tread of the most illustrious figures of Canadian history: Champlain, Maisonneuve,-whose house in Sillery still stands today-Frontenac, Laval, Montcalm and Wolfe, Cartier, Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier, to name but a few. The riding has been the site of the capital of French Canada and of the United Provinces of Canada. The Quebec conference preceding confederation was held there. And within its limits are to be found the provincial parliament buildings. In brief, my constituency is the birthplace of Canada and of Quebec.
While I am on that subject, Mr. Speaker, I would like to suggest to the government that because of the historical importance of that city and consequently of the attraction it has for Canadians and Americans, consideration might be given to some financial assistance to the municipality in the form of subsidies or otherwise, especially if we take into account the value of untaxed crown property in the city. In this way the municipal government would be in a position to discharge its heavy responsibilities and to increase the beauty and attractiveness of the city.
But the constituency of Quebec South has more than a historical interest. It also is part of modern Quebec whose progress since 1941 has been truly marvellous. Quebec offers unique advantages from the point of view of the establishment of new industries.
Quebec is one of the main shoe manufacturing districts in Canada. There you find more than 500 industries including bookbinding, tobacco, cigar and cigarettes, ladies' wear, agricultural products, food, furs, iron works, breweries, clothing, wood, pulp and paper.
The town of Sillery which is going to commemorate this year, between the 2nd and the 11th of June, the centenary of the incorporation of its municipality and of its school board, is a pleasant residential town which has grown rapidly since 1945 and of which my forefathers have been among the first settlers.
Now I would like to say a few words relating to some problems with which we are particularly concerned. One of the most important factors in the economic life of my constituency and of the city and district of Quebec is the harbour of Quebec.
The harbour of Quebec, as well as those of Halifax, Saint John, Chicoutimi, Montreal,
fMr. Power (Quebec South).]

Three Rivers, Churchill and Vancouver, is administered by the national harbours board, an institution which was established under chapter 42 of the Statutes of Canada for the year 1936.
Before the adoption of this legislation, the harbour of Quebec was state property and was administered by three government officials called the Quebec harbour commission. The change in the administration was made following Sir Alexander Gibb's recommendations, which he formulated after carrying on, at the request of the government, an inquiry into Canada's national harbours. His conclusions' were to the effect that the administrative system used was not satisfactory.
Consequently, the setting up of a central authority was proposed in order to co-ordinate direction and to supervise finance and works of a technical nature. Besides the central authority, the recommendation was also made to substitute for the harbour commissioners a local civil servant who would be called port manager. This official would have the direction of each harbour under the central authority. The National Harbours Board Act, chapter 42, statutes of 1936, gave effect to the above proposals.
Another recommendation, subordinate to the one above but which, unfortunately, was not put into effect, called for the setting up of a local harbour board which was to represent local interests and those that used the harbour, and would also help out the harbour master in matters of purely local concern.
The partial implementation of the Gibb report, as I have just indicated, resulted in a centralization which evoked almost unanimous criticism throughout the country, criticism which took the form of speeches and resolutions recorded from time to time in the orders of the day of this house.
The policy implemented as a result of the very nature of this act administered by the national harbours board has prevented the adoption of any corrective measure which could have been brought forward so as to stimulate the export of goods through the port of Quebec.
Consequently, Quebec harbour, though showing a balance sheet which is favourable in appearance, is not as widely used and known as it should be. We must not forget that the Quebec harbour commissioners did much to attract business to Quebec and that they fought to obtain concessions such as the preferential tariff on grain carried from Fort William to Quebec on the national transcontinental railway in 1921 and 1926. Since the disappearance of this harbour commission,

its functions of promoting trade in Quebec city have, to a certain extent, been assumed by the Quebec city chamber of commerce. Be that as it may, promotion carried out by that organization is obviously not as wide in scope as it would be if it were carried out by an authority having direct connections with the harbour.
The inherent weakness of the National Harbours Board Act as' it now stands is to be found in the fact that it is not within the terms of reference of the board, nor even of the local port manager, to promote competition between harbours. With regard to Quebec, it would seem that the harbour authorities are completely indifferent to any encouragement or stimulation of local business or to promotion or growth of regional and foreign trade. Indeed, the material assets of Quebec harbour have been so sadly neglected that they have deteriorated in an alarming way. Yet, recently, and as a result of representations made by the chamber of commerce, and supported by all federal members for that area in this house, an impressive program of reconstruction and improvements has been launched and it appears that, following instructions by the government, the national harbour board intends to recondition Quebec harbour. Though such action would be of great help, it would not be enough to ensure the prosperity of this port. It is essential that the recommendations of the Gibb report which I mentioned before, and which have not yet been passed-or some similar legislation-be added to the act so as to improve our domestic and foreign trade and to promote the development of the city by giving the harbour administration a more complete autonomy in co-operation with local business, industrial and labour interests.

Mr. Speaker, I crave your kind indulgence while I say a few brief words about my constituency, Quebec South. Its population is composed of about 85 per cent French speaking Canadians and 15 per cent English speaking Canadians, and of the 15 per cent half are Protestant and half Roman Catholic.
It is a marvellously beautiful county, as have testified the thousands and thousands of tourists who visit this section of Quebec and district every year. It has felt the tread of the most illustrious figures in Canadian history, such as Champlain, its founder; Maisonneuve, the founder of Montreal, whose house in Sillery still stands today; Laval, the founder of the oldest university on the continent; Frontenac, one of the greatest of its governors; Montcalm and Wolfe, whose glorious deaths are commemorated by the battlefields park and by numerous monuments and statues; Macdonald, Cartier and Sir Wilfrid Laurier, to name but a few. It is the site of the first permanent European settlement in Canada; in essence it is the cradle of Canada and the repository of a major part of its history. It is not surprising therefore, that I am deeply honoured and proud of the fact that I have been chosen to represent it in this house.
Mr. Speaker, whilst I am a newly arrived member of this house I am not a stranger to politics. Although I would not by any stretch of the imagination describe myself as an expert politician, for I have a great deal to learn, I have had some seven years of practical political experience as my father's assistant, and since adolescence I have been exposed more or less to the pratical and theoretical aspects of politics. As a result there has been developed in me the following, and possibly not surprising, theory with regard to my conduct as a member of this house and of the Liberal party.
I believe very strongly in the general political principles and objects of the Liberal party and in the practical manner in which they have been and are generally applied. In consequence of this, and of the fact that I was elected as a supporter of the Liberal party and of this government under the distinguished leadership of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, I owe loyalty to our party and to my chief. However, I do not believe that

Just as this government, as a Liberal government, has a dual responsibility, on the one hand to the party for the carrying out of the party platform when the occasion presents itself, and on the other hand and more importantly to the people of Canada toward whom it has a responsibility to discharge its functions irrespective of and despite its political commitments, so also I believe that I and every other hon. member of this house has a dual responsibility to the party whose principles he upholds and a responsibility as a member of this house for judging and passing on legislation which is brought down by the government. As in the case of father and son or brother and brother, I feel that any disagreement or criticism which in the discharge of my parliamentary obligations I may be obliged to express should not, or would not, in any way affect my standing as a member, of the Liberal party.
In this connection I would like to cite a paragraph from one of my last campaign speeches in which I expressed essentially the same thought:
In the course of my various discussions with you I have endeavoured to place before you the point of view of one who whilst strongly attached to the party to which he belongs, believes that no candidate should pledge himself in advance to the extent that he be precluded from exercising full liberty of action and the best of his judgment and discretion for the attitude which he will take in
all or any public question which may be presented to him during the course of his mandate as representative of the people.
Mr. Speaker, I have thought it best to avoid in this section of my speech discussion of particular issues of the day for which more appropriate occasions will arise. However, there is one subject now before this house in the form of two bills which I would like to touch upon before I close. I refer to the matter of bilingualism. Representing as I do a constituency which is by a large majority French speaking, and being myself bilingual, although there is room for improvement, I most strongly urge that this house should, as a principle, adopt the extension of bilingualism in the public service and public printing of Canada.
I do not mean that all English speaking or French speaking Canadians should be forced to speak each other's language, but I do feel that a French or English Canadian citizen should be able to obtain information or service from government publications or from selected civil service personnel wherever he may happen to be in Canada. I think this would go a long way toward increasing our sense of national unity.
Shall I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
What steps must an officer or airman who is not deemed to be married under Queen's regulations (air) article 205.20(2) (a) take to be deemed to be married?
Answer by: Mr. Campney:
If the marriage of the officer or airman has been dissolved or annulled within the meaning of QR(air) article 205.20 (2)(a)(i), nothing can alter his status under the article except, of course, his remarriage.
In respect to (2)(a)(ii), it might be possible for the officer or airman to bring a motion in court for cancellation of the maintenance decree. If successful, he could then substitute a personal contractual arrangement with his wife, e.g. "separation agreement". If there are children, it might be possible to have the court order altered to decree payments in respect of the children and not of the wife. In either of the foregoing cases, the officer or airman would be "deemed to be married" within the meaning of article 205.20.
